text:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott delivered one of the starkest warnings yet from a Republican to the AI industry, saying data center companies "dug their own grave" and deserve the backlash they're facing after failing to win community support.

Why it matters: Abbott is the latest governor to sharply change course on the AI data center boom he once enthusiastically courted, as local opposition becomes a potent political force.

Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who last year celebrated a $20 billion Amazon data center investment, imposed new restrictions this week.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat, last month ordered a one-year moratorium on hyperscaler data centers.

Catch up quick: Just last November, Abbott called Texas the "epicenter of AI development" as he joined Google to announce a $40 billion investment into three data center campuses.

In June, however, Abbott directed state regulators to make data centers pay the full cost of the electrical infrastructure they require and called for phasing out tax incentives.

Earlier this month, he ordered regulators to audit data centers seeking to connect to Texas' power grid before allowing the projects to move forward.

Zoom out: The backlash is quickly becoming a political problem for the AI industry.

Axios' Alex Isenstadt scooped last week that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned leading AI companies that voter anger over data centers was imperiling Republicans' chances of holding a critical Ohio Senate seat.

What he's saying: Abbott told telling ABC's Jonathan Karl on "This Week" that the backlash stems partly from the sheer speed of the buildout, and partly from developers moving into communities without first gaining support.

"Gaining the support of people in local communities is essential," Abbott said.

"They basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them," he continued. "And that's why they got the backlash they deserve."

Last week, Abbott told Fox News Sunday that fewer than 10% of data center companies had responded to a state request for information needed to project future power demand.

The intrigue: President Trump has taken aim at Abbott's approach, arguing "for Texas to say no to data centers is a mistake" because the industry "could be bigger than oil."

Skeptics have questioned the data center boom for some time; no one expected the problem to be red-state Republicans who suddenly realized they were at risk of losing an election over something voters vehemently opposed.

By the numbers: 61% of Americans now oppose construction of a new data center in their area, according to an Annenberg Public Policy Center survey last month, up from 49% in March.

The opposition crosses party lines: 69% of Democrats, 54% of Republicans and 53% of independents oppose new data centers in their area.

Between the lines: For years, the biggest questions around the massive AI buildout were whether the technology would live up to the hype, whether companies could secure enough chips and electricity, and whether the trillions in spending made sense.

Now the most immediate constraint is whether voters will allow the physical infrastructure necessary to power the AI boom.

Data centers bring enormous electricity demand, water use, transmission needs and industrial-scale construction into local communities.

They also provide fewer permanent jobs than the usual warehousing and manufacturing deals that usually earn tax incentives.

State of play: Data center spending has become large enough to matter for the broader American economy and central to the effort to stay ahead in the global AI race.

Texas is among the hottest data center markets, with developers initially attracted by a pro-business state that has ample supplies of natural gas and renewables, energy infrastructure, and lots of land.

The bottom line: If voter anger hardens into more moratoriums, slower permitting or abandoned projects, it could constrain the computing infrastructure AI companies are counting on and weaken one of the fastest-growing sources of U.S. investment.

The industry — and the entire economy — face a brutal reckoning if the political tone doesn't change, quickly.

text:
Synopsis

India's renewable energy growth demands more storage systems now. Domestic battery manufacturing capacity remains very low compared to future needs. This gap creates a reliance on imports for essential battery components. Experts caution against delaying renewable deployment due to this dependency. India aims to bridge this storage gap over the coming decade.

New Delhi: The growing renewable capacity has created an immediate need to scale up storage systems, industry stakeholders said, highlighting the huge gap between the demand and current capability to manufacture essential battery cell components.

Sharing their views with PTI, industry members have also cautioned against treating import dependence as a reason for slow deployment.

The experts' comments assume significance as India's domestic battery manufacturing currently accounts for less than 1 per cent (2 GWh) of its approximately 260 GWh demand pipeline from competitive tenders in 2026.

Read more: Delhi's master plan proposes solar, hydro power generation from canals, drains

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) and pumped storage projects are gaining importance as India expands renewable capacity to meet rising electricity demand and balance solar generation with peak demand, Sunkind India founder and Managing Director Hanish Gupta said.

Live Events

Batteries and other storage technologies are key to addressing the intermittency risk of solar power and unlocking its growth potential, Premier Energies Chief Business Officer Vinay Rustagi said.

Volks Energie CEO and co-founder Piyush Goyal said India's storage demand is running well ahead of what domestic cell manufacturing can supply, and that gap is a matter of years, not a few quarters.

"I would caution against treating import dependence as a reason to slow deployment. The grid needs storage now to firm up the renewable capacity we are adding, and pausing for a decade until cells are fully indigenous is not a choice we can make," he said.

Read more: Renewable energy developers get relief over delayed projects, with riders

In a public disclosure, NTPC Chairman Gurdeep Singh said that a storage system helps in both ways. During the daytime, RE power generated can be stored and used in the absence of sunlight.

He shared that NTPC has been allocated 5 GWh of battery energy storage capacity under the Viability Gap Funding scheme to optimise existing thermal generation and transmission infrastructure and ensure reliable and economical power supply during non-solar hours.

In its latest research last week, Wood Mackenzie said it would take more than a decade for India to achieve self-sufficiency in battery storage, as there is a huge gap between demand and current capability to manufacture essential battery cell components.

The gap leaves the country structurally dependent on imports even as policy ambition accelerates, it said, noting that India has just 2 GWh of commissioned cell manufacturing capacity as of 2026, against China's cumulative capacity of 2,695 GWh, which controls between 85 per cent and 98 per cent of global capacity across every major supply chain component, from cathode to anode, separator and electrolyte.

text:
Hungary will restart the first of three nuclear reactors it was forced to shut down due to the record low level of the Danube river, as the country looks to recover from an unprecedented energy crisis.

Authorities will restart block number 3 at its Paks nuclear plant Saturday evening, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said in a Facebook post. He credited rising river levels and emergency measures such as the construction of an underwater barrier in the river.

Rolling heat waves over the summer have dried up waterways across Europe, severely impacting Danube river flows and hindering the cooling systems at nuclear reactors. That has strained power grids, forcing Hungary to boost electricity imports and to ask both households and factories to voluntarily cut back on energy use.

Paks, which generates around 40% of Hungary’s electricity output, saw its output drop to as little as a tenth of its 2,000-megawatt capacity at one point, with only one of its four reactors running. It’s currently producing 481 megawatts.

text:
Huron-Clinton Metroparks is moving forward with a plan to remove part of the Flat Rock Dam, after a tentative agreement for the town of Flat Rock to purchase it fell through.

Metroparks offered last year to sell the dam for $5 and provide $4.5 million in funding to install a fish ladder and help fund the dam's operations. The dam is considered to be in fair condition but is classified as a high-hazard potential dam by the state, which means a failure could cause the loss of life or serious damage to critical infrastructure and the environment.

Flat Rock Mayor Steven Beller said after looking into the conditions around the dam and the costs of maintaining and operating it, which took about a year, the city council decided that buying the dam didn't feel like a financially responsible decision for a town as small as Flat Rock.

The city council voted unanimously not to buy the dam at its July 20 meeting.

"No one on council … wanted to take on the future financial responsibility. It wouldn't be fair to the residents," he said. "To take on $25-$35 million (in) future cost just isn't fiscally responsible."

Beller said the sentiment in town seems to be that most residents want the dam to stay.

The Flat Rock dam was built in the 1920s to supply hydroelectric power to a lamp factory owned by Ford. It assembled headlights and other lighting systems from 1923 to 1950, when the factory stopped operating.

Metroparks officials decided to move forward with partially removing the dam and installing rock arches at its Aug. 13 meeting. Under its plan, wetlands and water levels would be maintained in the impoundment behind the dam, preserving recreation and wildlife habitats, enhancing fish passage and reducing the risk of infrastructure failure.

“Our first priority has always been the health and safety of the region and the environment,” said CEO Amy McMillan in a statement.

Partial removal and installing rock arches will cost at least $13 million, according to Metroparks estimates. The design and permitting stages are expected to take about two years, the release said, which will include more chances for public feedback.

Permitting will follow design, and Metroparks will seek bids from construction contractors. The body has about $920,000 in grant funding for design and permitting from the National Oceanic Administration Fisheries Regional Partnership, and Metroparks plans to pursue additional grants.

Metroparks staff originally recommended partial removal and putting in rock arches in the summer of 2025, but the board chose to delay voting to renew its attempt to sell the dam to Flat Rock.

"I think residents are understanding that no matter what, it's going to be a long process," Beller said.

text:
A cooperation forum focused on Danzhou's new energy industrial chain drew nearly 100 companies, investors and industry groups to Shanghai on Friday, as the Hainan Free Trade Port's industrial core pushes to build a clean-energy hub and cut carbon emissions.

The Danzhou modern energy system industrial chain cooperation matchmaking meeting, themed around the pilot free trade port's "model room" advantages, featured talks on green certification, low-carbon manufacturing and export channels. Several key projects were signed on-site.

Danzhou Yangpu, which calls itself a free trade port "showcase" and industrial center, is accelerating efforts to upgrade its energy structure while coordinating green industrial transformation, according to local officials.

"Green and low-carbon development is a defining feature of high-quality growth in the Hainan Free Trade Port," said Chen Yang, mayor of Danzhou and director of the Yangpu Economic Development Zone Administration. He said Danzhou is focusing on three areas - clean power generation, modern power grids and clean heat sources - and is building a full offshore wind industry chain covering equipment manufacturing, power generation and hydrogen-ammonia-methanol utilization. The city is also moving ahead with two flagship projects to bring nuclear power and nuclear steam into Yangpu and is developing a zero-carbon industrial park.

Chen said Danzhou's new energy sector is entering a "golden window" for industrial agglomeration and value growth. The city aims to have a basic clean-energy supply system in place by 2030, providing sufficient, stable and traceable energy. He invited companies to invest and take part in the full new-energy chain, leveraging local resources, free trade port policy advantages and global market links.

Siemens Energy, which supplied heavy-duty gas turbine combined-cycle units to Yangpu Power Plant in the 1990s, formally established a Hainan company in Yangpu this year and broke ground on a turbine assembly and service center. "Two major strategic opportunities - the construction of the Hainan Free Trade Port and the green energy transition - are converging here," said Chen Sihui, vice president of Siemens Energy. She said the company will deepen cooperation in gas power, grid technology, offshore wind and energy digitalization.

Several key players are advancing projects. Hainan Power Grid is building a new power system with zoned distribution and layered operations for Danzhou. By 2030, the city is expected to have a relatively independent modern grid, with Hainan Nuclear Power directly supplying 220-kilovolt lines via a "point-to-network" model, giving local companies access to more traceable green electricity. Clean-energy producers including Huaneng Changjiang Nuclear Power will support the nuclear-power and nuclear-steam initiatives.

Cosco Shipping and other logistics firms are exploring green shipping, low-carbon logistics and carbon-accounting for transport to align with Danzhou's low-carbon industrial plans. The goal is to create a full loop - green energy, green manufacturing, green logistics, green certification and green exports - that helps companies meet international carbon standards.

Four rounds of project signings took place during the forum. The deals cover testing and certification, low-carbon services, green power supply, equipment manufacturing, hydrogen energy, power trading and integrated energy services.

Organizers said the strong turnout reflects market confidence in Danzhou Yangpu's new-energy strategy, the free trade port's policy strengths and the region's low-carbon growth prospects.

title: Heat waves are stress-testing data center power plans - MarketScale
description:

For data center operators and the utilities that serve them, that spread is the story.
It also noted a key wrinkle for large-load planners: PJM and Texas sit at the center of the country’s data center buildout, and data centers are a small but growing portion of load in SPP.
PJM said that demand would have broken a 20-year-old record if not for conservation programs that reduced load, according to E&E News.

text:
PJM Interconnection’s early-July heat wave and Texas’ mid-July heat wave were the same category of problem, record air-conditioning load. The operational outcome was nothing alike. PJM saw prices spike above $2,000 per megawatt-hour around its July 2 peak, while the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) hit a July 22 demand record without emergency actions and with real-time prices around $29/MWh, according to E&E News.

For data center operators and the utilities that serve them, that spread is the story. The AI infrastructure boom is arriving in a climate regime that is already producing more frequent, sharper summer peaks. The practical question is no longer whether grids can “handle” large loads in the abstract, it’s which markets can deliver predictable capacity and predictable pricing during the same late-day hours when both people and servers are pulling hard.

Heat peaks are turning into a siting and contracting variable, not a weather anecdote

E&E News, reporting by Benjamin Storrow, described three U.S. regions where extreme heat pushed demand to historical highs: PJM (mid-Atlantic), Southwest Power Pool (Great Plains), and ERCOT (Texas). It also noted a key wrinkle for large-load planners: PJM and Texas sit at the center of the country’s data center buildout, and data centers are a small but growing portion of load in SPP.

GridStatus.io analyst Abby Lestina told E&E News that large loads are coming online and that heat is making the impact easier to see. That framing matters for enterprise operators because it ties two planning timelines together: multi-year interconnection and construction schedules for new campuses, and the immediate reality that heat-driven peaks can show up any summer.

PJM said that demand would have broken a 20-year-old record if not for conservation programs that reduced load, according to E&E News. For operators writing requirements for colocation expansions or self-built campuses, that’s a signal that “availability” increasingly includes curtailment pathways: contractual demand response, utility-managed conservation programs, or on-site load shedding that can be triggered on short notice.

ERCOT’s solar and battery fleet showed what “peak help” looks like at 6 p.m.

The clean-energy narrative around heat events often collapses into a simplistic debate about whether solar can perform after dark. E&E News reported that a U.S. Department of Energy social media post argued that solar did not deliver power after dark during PJM’s peak, prompting pushback from clean-energy advocates and coverage elsewhere.

But the more useful operational comparison in E&E News’ reporting is intra-day timing and controllability. When ERCOT demand peaked around 6 p.m. on July 22, solar was generating roughly a third of the grid’s power, according to E&E News. The story also credited Texas’ large solar and battery buildout as the key difference versus PJM and SPP, which it described as having less solar and storage.

For buyers, “solar share at peak” is an actionable metric because it points to what should be validated in a feasibility study: the local net-load curve, the late-afternoon ramp rate, and the amount of storage that can be dispatched through the top 10 system peaks. If the peak is shifting later in the evening as heat lingers, solar alone changes energy economics but may not change capacity risk unless storage is in the stack.

The global transition milestone is real, but grids are still local

A National Wildlife Federation Facebook post pointed to a separate, upbeat milestone: globally, solar and wind have together produced more electricity than coal for the first time. Even as the post did not provide the underlying dataset, the claim reflects a widely discussed direction of travel in the energy transition.

What the U.S. heat-week experience adds, per E&E News, is that the enterprise consequence shows up at the interconnection and tariff level. A global generation milestone doesn’t tell a hyperscaler whether a specific utility territory can firm up 100 MW of new load without forcing years of network upgrades, or whether a market will expose that load to scarcity pricing during the hottest 20 hours of the year.

E&E News also reported that Dominion Energy executives told investors that nine of the utility’s top 10 power-consumption days have occurred this year, with eight of its highest summer peaks occurring in just over two months. Virginia hosts the world’s largest concentration of data centers, and Dominion’s territory is a bellwether for what happens when the largest load cluster in the country meets sharper weather extremes.

Southwest Power Pool’s experience points to a broader footprint issue. E&E News cited preliminary U.S. Energy Information Administration data showing SPP demand reached nearly 58 gigawatts on July 27, the highest level recorded in EIA’s preliminary power data. SPP also had to implement emergency measures across parts of the Great Plains, E&E News reported. That matters for operators considering “second-tier” markets for cost reasons: lower land and fiber costs don’t automatically translate into lower power-system risk.

What large-load developers and procurement teams should pressure-test this quarter

description:

text:
Research from two University of California campuses is casting doubt on a familiar criticism of electric vehicles. The study suggests that continuing to drive the gas-powered car you already own is not automatically the better choice for the climate.

Their modeling found that, for most drivers, making the switch earlier can reduce emissions. That means retiring a still-functional gas vehicle and replacing it with an EV may provide a meaningful climate benefit.

Here's what to know

According to CleanTechnica, citing research from UC Santa Barbara's Roland Geyer and UC Santa Cruz's J. Elliott Campbell, scrapping a working combustion vehicle and moving to an EV produced lower emissions 92% of the time.

To determine whether switching to an EV sooner or keeping an existing gas-powered car on the road would result in fewer emissions, researchers compared the environmental impact of continuing to operate a functional gas vehicle with permanently retiring it and replacing it with a battery-electric vehicle.

In one representative case, as CleanTechnica reported, swapping a production-weighted SUV on the average U.S. grid lowered total emissions by 44% over 16 years when the gas vehicle was retired after year two. The added emissions from building the replacement EV were generally offset after about three years of cleaner driving.

The key variable was how much fuel the old vehicle would still burn, not the emissions from making the battery. Differences in fuel use and driving efficiency mattered more than even a wide range of battery-production pollution.

Still, the study was not a blanket endorsement of getting rid of every older car. Very lightly driven vehicles, efficient hybrids, and some plug-in hybrids may not provide a climate benefit if they are replaced too soon, particularly in places with dirtier electricity grids.

More background

The slogan "the greenest car is the one already built" leaves out an important timing issue, the outlet reported. The manufacturing emissions tied to an existing gas car have already happened, so the bigger climate question is how much more pollution that vehicle will create if it stays in service.

In the United States, many households rely on cars for work, school, medical appointments, and everyday errands. Any effort to encourage older vehicles to be scrapped has to weigh the climate benefits against the reality that affordable used cars remain essential for many families.

EVs can also come with clear financial benefits. They usually cost less to fuel than gas-powered vehicles and often require less routine maintenance because they do not need oil changes and have fewer moving parts that wear down over time.

A more effective approach would target the highest-polluting vehicles first while still preserving affordable transportation options.

What can be done?

According to CleanTechnica, the research points to the value of more targeted vehicle-retirement incentives.

Rather than offering the same payout for any older vehicle, policymakers could focus on high-mileage pickups, inefficient SUVs, and other gas guzzlers likely to create the most future emissions.

For households considering a switch, the economics can improve further with home charging. Charging an EV at home often costs less than using public chargers, but basic Level 1 charging tends to be slow. Qmerit provides free, instant installation estimates for faster Level 2 home charger installations.

The study also suggests that large fleets could play an outsized role. Rental companies, delivery services, governments, and corporations tend to log heavy mileage, so, as CleanTechnica noted, electrifying them early could cut emissions quickly while also moving more used EVs into the market within three to five years.

A stronger secondhand EV market could give more drivers access to cleaner transportation without requiring them to buy brand-new vehicles.

text:
A new youth program trained 16 students from southwest Detroit, Ecorse, and River Rouge to be environmental justice advocates.

The 10-month Eden Park Environmental Justice Youth Ambassador Program was provided by the nonprofit Tri-City Community Development Corporation.

Many of the students have asthma, believed to be linked to pollution in their communities, which are some of Michigan's most pollution-burdened areas.

The program aims to empower young people to improve their communities' quality of life and consider careers in environmental justice.

On the afternoon of Aug. 12, in a festively decorated room in the lower level of Detroit’s Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History, Makayla Nellum wore a look of joy on her face while sitting at a table reserved for a special group of young people that have been engaged in an activity with local, national and global implications.

A few minutes later, the 15-year-old's smile widened just a little bit more when it was announced that these young special guests, seated at two tables front and center of the room, would be served lunch first.

Nellum and the others, all sporting vibrant green shirts, were more than deserving of the VIP treatment because they represented the first graduating class from the Eden Park Environmental Justice Youth Ambassador Program.

The program, provided by the nonprofit Tri-City Community Development Corporation (CDC), brought middle and high school students together from the 48217, 48218 and 48229 ZIP codes for 10 months of training, amounting to 80 hours, that prepared them to become environmental justice advocates and educators in their own communities.

"Doing a project with people from three different cities (southwest Detroit, Ecorse and River Rouge) is something I had never done before," Nellum, a rising junior at Ecorse High School, said. "But we all came together and completed our goal."

To complete their goal of becoming environmental justice youth ambassadors, the 16 girls and boys — ranging in age from 12-19 — that completed the inaugural program under the tutelage of community and environmental organizer Siwatu-Salama Ra, each learned and began to practice the 17 Principles of Environmental Justice, which were drafted and adopted by delegates of the First National People Of Color Environmental Leadership Summit in 1991.

The 17 principles can be viewed as a call to action to bring about environmental equity across the planet, including the 48217 ZIP code in southwest Detroit, which often is cited by researchers as Michigan's most pollution-burdened community due to the cluster of industrial activity in the surrounding area.

The fact that 16 local youths — 80% of whom have been diagnosed with asthma thought to be linked to pollution in their communities — have joined the action to improve their quality of life and the lives of many others also was a reason for the Rev. Dr. Alex Hill to celebrate at the Wright Museum.

"I got involved in environmental issues out of southwest Detroit about 25 years ago and I did not know the extent of the toxins in the air,” said Hill, board chairman for Tri-City CDC, which is an extension of the outreach ministry performed by New Mount Hermon Missionary Baptist Church, where Hill has been pastor for more than 30 years.

“Flint got so much notoriety regarding what was going on with their water. But little did people know that some of the same toxins that plagued the water in Flint also plagues the air in southwest Detroit," he said. "I said to (U.S.) Congresswoman (Rashida) Tlaib (a southwest Detroit native and 1994 graduate of Southwestern High School) some years ago that you can pump in fresh water, but you can’t pump in fresh air.

"That’s why the Eden Park Community Project is so important, because we’re in the process of trying to build a park (where the former Mark Twain Elementary School once stood at 12001 Gleason in Detroit) with air-purifying trees and green spaces to help mitigate the astronomical death rates and other health issues that have been linked to pollution in that area. And that's why the involvement of our young people is so important as well, because from the time they got into the program and did the toxic tour through their community, we have seen their excitement and how troubled they were to find out that they’re living in the midst of all this.

"It’s an issue that is going to require a lot of time and attention, but our young people have embraced this challenge and we’re excited that we have new leaders coming forward.”

Roughly an hour after Hill's statement, the young people that the Reverend spoke of — the same young people who made their views on mental health, housing security and access to medical care known this spring during a community meeting in River Rouge presented by the Sierra Club on the outcome of the EPA's Clean Air Act lawsuit over Zug Island pollution — shared their impressions about the Eden Park Environmental Justice Youth Ambassador Program.

"This program has given us knowledge that we can share with our community and peers," said Noah Burrel, a rising senior at Ecorse High School, where he has excelled in the classroom and as a member of the basketball and baseball teams. "We will never forget this experience and we will take this knowledge and use it to better our community."

Burrel was deserving of extra kudos, given that he took the courageous step to be the first student speaker, which broke the ice for the students that spoke afterward. However, after the ceremony concluded, Dr. Alicia Renee Farris made it crystal clear that she has been equally impressed with all of the Eden Park Environmental Justice Youth Ambassadors.

"I am so grateful to these young people for the amount of energy and passion they put into the work,” said Tri-City CDC executive board member Farris, who worked closely with all of the students that participated in the inaugural program. “They invested 80 hours of their time, and I held them highly accountable for every hour and every activity because leadership requires much.

“In our group we had students that are athletes on sports teams, as well as students that participate in dance competitions, so they came tired after their practices, which demonstrated their perseverance and commitment. And with the training that each young person has received they can advocate for themselves and others who are unable to advocate for themselves.

“We also want them to consider environmental justice as a career path to green jobs, while becoming leaders in the field. Not often have we seen people of color heavily invested in this, but we have certainly suffered from what has taken place in our communities in the past. So, now we have birthed something that will allow our young people to be a part of the solution and lead a life of dedication to their community.”

Farris' sentiment was echoed by Dr. Loretta Gary Smith, who was literally rejoicing for two during the graduation ceremony because of her husband, the late Rev. Dr. William J. Smith, who co-founded Tri-City CDC and was a tireless advocate for young people in southwest Detroit, River Rouge and Ecorse.

"Kids were his (Smith's husband) passion and that came through in all of the after-school and summer programs that he helped to put on," said Loretta Smith, Tri-City CDC's executive director, who, along with Farris and other community activists, also was honored during the ceremony at the Wright museum by Alisha Barnes, president of Just Transition Team MI-River Rouge.

"I know he is smiling down on us because he also spent a lot of time helping us get the plot of land for the community where Eden Park will be constructed. As an organization, we just want to continue working for the community, while also having the flexibility to evolve with the times, and I know our young people will help us to do that."

'Strengthening the family’s quality of life'

What: Tri-City Community Development Corporation (CDC)

Mission: Since 1999, Tri-City CDC, an extension of the outreach ministry performed by New Mount Hermon Missionary Baptist Church and the brainchild of the Rev. Dr. Alex R. Hill and the late Rev. Dr. William J. Smith, has been committed to empowering residents in southwest Detroit, River Rouge and Ecorse. The nonprofit addresses vital human needs through the development and implementation of community initiatives that strengthen families and enrich their quality of life. In addition to providing a host of services for families, Tri-City CDC’s initiatives focus on “seniors, opportunity training and youth programs.”

Recent event: A graduation celebration at the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History honoring graduates of the inaugural Eden Park Environmental Justice Youth Ambassador Program. The graduates representing middle and high school students from Ecorse, Detroit and River Rouge, who each completed the 80-hour leadership-development program across 10 months, were: Noah Burrel, DaViona Calhoun, DaZaria Calhoun, Breion DeWitt, Ariya Harrington, Remiya Fowlkes Harrington, Braylin Hill, Nala Lanae Hill, Bethesda Samai Monrroy, Makayla Nellum, Kori Perry, Gabrielle Steele, Amirrah Thomas, Tavarie Warren, Terrence Warren, Treiden Warren.

Learn more: For more information about the Tri-City CDC’s initiatives, including the ongoing Ten Bring $Ten fundraiser, which asks people to give $10 and then recruit 10 other people to donate $10 each to support the Eden Park Community Project, please visit https://tri-citycdc.org and https://edenpark-cdp.org

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy has told X-energy it will receive up to $1 billion in additional federal funding for its small modular reactor project with Dow in Seadrift, Texas. CEO Clay Sell disclosed the award on an earnings call, saying total public support for the project has now reached up to $2.15 billion since 2021.

DOE awards X-energy up to $1 billion in additional funding

The new grant comes through the DOE’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program—ARDP, for short. Sell announced it during an earnings call, and the DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy confirmed it shortly after. Total federal support for the Dow–X-energy collaboration now stands at up to $2.15 billion—a figure that makes the federal government’s confidence in this project hard to miss.

That level of public investment stands out even by nuclear energy standards, where large capital requirements are simply part of the territory.

Rather than funding research alone, the program uses cost-shared partnerships with private companies to push designs from paper toward real commercial deployment.

Cost-share requirements and funding structure

The $1 billion doesn’t come free and clear. Like X-energy’s original ARDP award in 2021, this new funding requires a 50/50 cost-share—for every federal dollar, X-energy and its partners have to put up one of their own. The DOE uses this structure deliberately, spreading financial risk between government and industry rather than placing it entirely on taxpayers.

For X-energy, the stakes are direct. Sell told investors the DOE grant “is our largest source of revenue at our current stage of development.” That’s a candid admission, and it tells you exactly how central federal support is to keeping this project moving.

Requiring industry to put real money on the table filters out projects without genuine commercial backing. It also lowers the barrier for emerging reactor technologies that still need a push to reach viability.

Project scope: Four Xe-100 reactors at Dow’s Seadrift plant

The funding targets a specific goal: installing four Xe-100 small modular reactors at Dow’s Seadrift Operations plant on the Texas Gulf Coast. Together, those four reactors would generate 320 megawatts of electricity and industrial steam—enough to power a major industrial facility at scale.

Seadrift is a petrochemical and plastics plant. The reactors are designed to replace existing energy and steam units currently running on aging fossil-fuel infrastructure—not a minor upgrade, but a direct swap of carbon-intensive sources for nuclear power at an active industrial site.

Sell described the project’s potential in broader terms, calling it the expected “first grid-scale advanced nuclear reactor deployed to serve an industrial site in North America.” If that holds, Seadrift won’t just be a power project—it’ll be a proof of concept for industrial nuclear energy across the continent.

Regulatory progress and operational timeline

Regulatory progress has been steady, though there’s still a ways to go. The project cleared an environmental assessment milestone from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission—a meaningful step in the federal review process—and Dow and X-energy submitted a construction permit application to the NRC last year.

That review is still ongoing. Not unusual for a project this complex, but real regulatory hurdles remain before any ground breaks on the reactor installations.

Operations are targeted for the early 2030s. That puts the project roughly a decade out from its initial 2021 funding to potential first power—a pace that reflects both the scale of the undertaking and how deliberate nuclear licensing tends to be in the U.S.

Background: DOE’s advanced reactor demonstration program

The ARDP was created to solve a problem the U.S. nuclear industry had struggled with for decades: actually getting next-generation reactor designs built. Rather than funding research alone, the program uses cost-shared partnerships with private companies to push designs from paper toward real commercial deployment.

X-energy first received ARDP funding in 2021, making Seadrift one of the program’s longest-running active awards. The fact that the relationship has lasted this long—and that the DOE just committed another billion—signals continued confidence in both the Xe-100 design and the Dow partnership as a workable commercial path.

Small modular reactors sit at the center of the DOE’s strategy for rebuilding domestic nuclear capacity. Unlike conventional large-scale plants, SMRs require less upfront capital and can be sited closer to industrial or remote energy users—a practical fit for applications like Seadrift, where a traditional gigawatt-scale plant wouldn’t be necessary or feasible.

320 MW of electricity and steam

Here’s where things stand: X-energy has secured up to $1 billion in new federal funding through the DOE’s ARDP, bringing total public support for the Dow partnership to up to $2.15 billion since 2021. The money will fund four Xe-100 reactors at Dow’s Seadrift facility, producing 320 megawatts of electricity and steam while replacing fossil-fuel energy sources.

text:
Accountability for NOx exposure

“California sues Trump administration to preserve clean air rules,” (mercedsunstar.com, June 22)

As a doctorally-prepared nurse practitioner working in occupational and environmental health, I spend my career looking at the space between environmental exposure and diagnosis, including researching the diagnostic gaps around Valley Fever, a soil-borne fungal disease dispersed by windblown dust, that disproportionately affects Central Valley communities.

I am writing about a different exposure risk that follows the same pattern: the Central Valley is home to some of the most heavily trafficked freight corridors in California, running through communities that already carry a disproportionate air quality burden. The current Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rulemaking on heavy-duty truck NOx emissions will directly affect the health of patients and workers here.

Manufacturers have not disputed that pollution controls to reduce NOx emissions are achievable. The disagreement is over whether they should be required to deploy what they’ve already built. It’s a question of whether the EPA will enforce commitments manufacturers have already made or let political pressure erode them.

Central Valley communities living alongside these freight corridors don’t get to opt out of the exposure. The EPA shouldn’t let manufacturers opt out of accountability.

Ayomidamope (Ayo) Adebiyi

Merced

Upcoming programming at Fresno museum

“Armenian museum marks independence of Nagorno-Karabakh with special guest,” (fresnobee.com, Sept. 2, 2016)

On Sept. 2, the Armenian Museum of Fresno will commemorate the 35th anniversary of Artsakh’s Declaration of Independence with an evening of history, photography and personal testimony.

For Armenians, Artsakh is more than a place on the map; it’s an ancestral homeland tied to centuries of faith, culture and memory. In recent years, its indigenous Armenian population was uprooted, adding another painful chapter to a long history of displacement and ethnic cleansing.

Guest of honor Archbishop Barkev Mardirossian served the Armenian people of Artsakh for over three decades through war, independence and upheaval. Photographer Ezras Tellalian will share photography documenting civilian life during the 2020 war, and author Ashot Poghosyan will discuss his biography of Archbishop Pargev Martirosyan, former Primate of Artsakh.

These stories speak to universal questions of homeland and what is lost when people are separated from their ancestral land. The evening opens Armenian Cultural Month, which continues through October as the museum marks its 25th anniversary. We invite the broader Fresno community to learn and reflect with us throughout the month.

Varoujan Der Simonian

Armenian Museum of Fresno, director

Appalling

“Haitians express ‘profound fear’ as Temporary Protected Status deadline nears,” (fresnobee.com, July 23)

Every American should be appalled by the Trump administration’s action to revoke temporary protected status (TPS) for Haitians in the U.S. What is more appalling is that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is now forcing Haitians in the U.S. who have lost their TPS status to wear ankle monitors.

Sean P Boyd

Fresno

Leo ICT Cables PLC has upgraded its lithium-ion battery manufacturing facility with automated systems, robotics and modern production technologies, targeting improved capacity, precision and product safety.

The upgraded facility at Kaliakair Hi-Tech Park in Gazipur can produce around 400 HQ-branded lithium-ion battery packs daily across nearly 40 product categories, according to a press release.

The automated production line will manufacture battery packs for renewable energy storage systems, electric vehicles, uninterruptible power supply and instant power supply systems, data centres, electric three-wheelers and other industrial applications.

Leo ICT said it had manufactured and marketed HQ lithium-ion battery packs in Bangladesh for the past two years.

The company said the latest upgrade was intended to meet growing domestic demand, improve product consistency and bring its manufacturing processes in line with international standards.

It expects automated production to enhance operational safety, manufacturing precision and overall productivity.

Leo ICT said expanding domestic battery production could reduce reliance on imported products, save foreign currency, attract investment in technology-driven industries and create skilled employment.

The company also expects local production to support the development of related industries within Bangladesh's manufacturing sector.

It said the investment aligned with government initiatives to promote renewable energy, strengthen domestic industrial capacity and generate employment.

Experts cited in the release said long-term global competitiveness would require sustained investment in research and development, international quality certification, product safety, technology transfer and skilled workforce development.

title: H1 2026 U.S. grid additions favor solar plus batteries - MarketScale
description:
The numbers that change how “new capacity” should be read in 2026 Inside Climate News reported that utility-scale solar led H1 2026 additions by both project count and capacity.
The EIA data show 207 solar projects entered service, compared with 95 battery projects.
Inside Climate News reported that the three largest natural-gas plant categories together added 2,707 MW in H1 2026.
Inside Climate News itself flagged the usual caveats: solar output is intermittent, and many gas plants run only during peaks.
Texas led, and its mix leaned more heavily on batteries and gas than many other states, Inside Climate News wrote.
text:
A simple count of what actually entered service in the U.S. power sector in the first half of 2026 points to a procurement reality operators are already living: solar is the default new-build, and batteries are showing up right behind it. The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s monthly generator inventory (EIA-860M) shows 368 utility-scale plants began operating from January through June 2026, and most were utility-scale solar, according to an Inside Climate News analysis published Aug. 13, 2026.

For enterprise energy managers, this isn’t a climate narrative. It’s a contracting and risk-management one. If more of the country’s new capacity is solar paired with storage, then the practical questions move toward deliverable energy in the hours that matter to load, dispatch rights, and how storage duration is specified in PPAs and tolling structures.

The numbers that change how “new capacity” should be read in 2026

Inside Climate News reported that utility-scale solar led H1 2026 additions by both project count and capacity. The EIA data show 207 solar projects entered service, compared with 95 battery projects. On a capacity basis, Inside Climate News pegged solar additions at 11,458 MW and batteries at 8,207 MW for the first six months of 2026.

Natural gas was present, but nowhere near solar and storage in what actually came online. Inside Climate News reported that the three largest natural-gas plant categories together added 2,707 MW in H1 2026. It also noted that combined-cycle gas, despite substantial announced capacity in development, accounted for just three projects entering service in that period.

That split matters because enterprise operators often see “MW added” reported as if it’s an apples-to-apples reliability story. It isn’t. Inside Climate News itself flagged the usual caveats: solar output is intermittent, and many gas plants run only during peaks. The job for operations, IT, and procurement teams is turning those caveats into contract language and performance metrics that finance and risk can live with.

Why capacity factor and duration are creeping into commercial terms

The most pointed operator takeaway from the Ars Technica forum discussion of the same topic is that nameplate capacity obscures how much energy a resource delivers over time. In the thread, one participant emphasized “capacity factor” and cited typical averages of about 25% for grid-scale solar and about 35% for onshore wind. The same post noted many battery installations are designed around roughly four hours at rated output, which is a duration choice, not a generation source.

In practical procurement terms, that’s the gap that’s widening in 2026: organizations that historically benchmarked deals by $/MW or total installed MW are being pushed toward $/MWh delivered in defined windows, along with explicit storage duration, round-trip efficiency, degradation assumptions, and cycling limits. Batteries showing up at 8,207 MW in just six months, as Inside Climate News reported, indicates that project developers and offtakers are already treating “solar plus storage” as a combined product in many regions.

The operational pitfall is treating batteries as generic firming. Four-hour systems can be excellent for shifting solar into evening peaks, but they solve a different problem than a multi-day resilience requirement at a critical facility, or winter peak needs in certain regions. That difference is starting to determine which contract structures work: a vanilla PPA may be fine for energy, while capacity and performance guarantees often need additional products or riders.

Where the build is happening, and what it signals for portfolio planning

Geography matters as much as technology mix. Inside Climate News reported that three states, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, accounted for about half of the country’s new generating capacity in H1 2026. Texas led, and its mix leaned more heavily on batteries and gas than many other states, Inside Climate News wrote.

Texas alone added 3,067 MW of batteries, 2,311 MW of utility-scale solar, and 1,154 MW of natural gas combustion turbines or natural gas internal combustion engines in H1 2026, according to Inside Climate News’ summary of the EIA data. The article tied that mix to policies that prioritize gas and battery construction to bolster reliability during high demand.

For multi-site operators, that’s the conditional relevance that matters. If facilities sit in markets that compensate capacity, ancillary services, or peak-shaving explicitly, expect storage to be a first-class procurement item and expect project developers to bring more complex offers. If operations are concentrated in markets without those revenue streams, “solar plus storage” pricing and availability can look very different, even if the underlying hardware costs are converging.

The other geographic signal is that outlier mega-projects can distort category headlines. Inside Climate News said the largest additions included the SunZia Wind South and SunZia Wind North projects in New Mexico, a combined 3,650 MW that it described as the largest wind farms in the country, and framed them as long-in-development projects rather than evidence of a fresh onshore wind boom.

That distinction matters for buyers using public commissioning data to forecast supplier capacity, EPC availability, and interconnection queues. A handful of large projects can move the capacity totals, but the operational pattern is being set by the smaller and mid-size solar projects that are “almost everywhere,” as Energy Innovation senior fellow Eric Gimon told Inside Climate News, and that are frequently paired with batteries.

The first half of 2026 delivered a blunt data point for anyone planning power supply, site selection, or resiliency: batteries are now entering service at a scale that’s hard to treat as a pilot category.

From January through June, 368 utility-scale plants began operating in the U.S., dominated by solar and battery projects, according to an analysis by Inside Climate News based on the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s EIA-860M generator dataset. Solar led on both project count and capacity, but storage was close enough behind to change how operators should think about “new capacity” when they’re writing contracts and forecasts.

Inside Climate News counted 207 utility-scale solar projects and 95 battery projects reaching commercial operation in the first half of 2026, using EIA’s monthly generator updates. After those two categories, the pipeline thins quickly: natural gas combustion turbines (22 projects) and natural gas internal combustion engines (21) followed, with onshore wind at 9 projects and combined-cycle gas at just 3.

Capacity tells the same story. Inside Climate News reported 11,458 MW of new utility-scale solar and 8,207 MW of batteries coming online in the six-month period, versus 5,473 MW of onshore wind, a figure heavily influenced by the SunZia buildout in New Mexico. The three largest categories of new gas plants added 2,707 MW combined in that timeframe, the outlet reported from the EIA dataset.

That distinction is where enterprise operators can get tripped up if they treat the EIA table as a simple scoreboard. Solar MW and battery MW don’t behave like combined-cycle MW. Inside Climate News flagged the basic caveat, solar doesn’t produce at night, while many gas peakers run only during narrow windows of high demand. The capacity labels can be comparable on paper and very different in delivered energy and reliability value.

Why “nameplate MW” is a weaker planning unit in 2026

An Ars Technica forum discussion of the same “so much solar” reporting put a finer point on the metric problem: a commenter noted capacity factor as a way to translate nameplate capacity into delivered energy, citing typical averages of about 25% for grid-scale solar and about 35% for onshore wind, and observing that many battery installations are designed around peak windows with a nominal runtime of roughly four hours. Those are rough heuristics, not EIA statistics, but they reflect the modeling move many planners now need to make explicitly.

For operations and procurement teams, the practical shift is to stop letting MW be the only unit that makes it into the statement of work. Battery duration, round-trip efficiency, augmentation schedules, and dispatch limits will determine whether a “400 MW battery” actually behaves as a capacity hedge for a data center campus, a manufacturing plant with a fixed demand charge, or a fleet depot with a predictable charging block.

Inside Climate News pointed to one large example that mixes the categories: the Green River Energy Center in Utah, described as 800 MW total, split between 400 MW of solar and 400 MW of batteries. Pairings like that are becoming a default build pattern because they can deliver a shaped output profile that better matches peak pricing and peak reliability needs than standalone solar.

Geography matters: Texas’ build mix is a reference case for peak-risk strategy

Where these projects came online is as operationally important as what they are, because congestion, curtailment risk, and interconnection lead times are local. Inside Climate News reported that Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona accounted for about half of new U.S. generating capacity in the first half of 2026.

Texas led, and its mix is a concrete planning reference for any operator exposed to ERCOT-style peak dynamics. Inside Climate News’ EIA-based tally put Texas additions at 3,067 MW of batteries, 2,311 MW of utility-scale solar, and 1,154 MW of new capacity from natural gas combustion turbines or natural gas internal combustion engines in the first half of 2026. The outlet also described Texas policy choices as prioritizing gas and batteries to support reliability during high-demand periods.

This matters for enterprise energy buyers for a simple reason: the hedge value of a PPA or tolling agreement increasingly depends on when and where it can deliver, not only what the levelized cost looks like. In regions where solar is plentiful, the risk shifts toward midday price collapses and curtailment. Storage changes the shape, but it also introduces a new constraint, duration, that has to be priced and contracted.

What to put in front of procurement, facilities, and grid teams this quarter

The EIA-860M data is a generator inventory, not an enterprise playbook. But the first-half 2026 mix, as interpreted by Inside Climate News and debated in Ars Technica’s technical back-and-forth, points to a few concrete work items for operators who buy power, manage peak exposure, or write interconnection and resiliency plans.
