title: Why America's Energy Grid Has To Change — And What It Means For Wyoming
description:
Either America rebuilds its energy grid fast, or it will hand the coming AI revolution — and the billions in economic impact that comes with it — to foreign countries, some of whom aren’t America’s friends.
Priority Power is a major energy solutions and transmission management provider in North America.
Tai agreed to speak to Cowboy State Daily after the private party about what America’s energy grid needs in the next century to continue leading the world, as well as how a brave new digital asset world could benefit Wyoming.
“We need to make some fundamental changes to how we govern, how we regulate, and how we construct our next-generation (energy) production and grid,” Tai said.
But the race to rebuild America’s grid is already, in some respects, off to the races to capture their slice of this emerging new economy.
text:
To the “tech bros,” the future is simple. Either America rebuilds its energy grid fast, or it will hand the coming AI revolution — and the billions in economic impact that comes with it — to foreign countries, some of whom aren’t America’s friends.

Ask around Wyoming coffee shops about AI, data centers, Bitcoin mines and the energy transformation all that’s going to require, and you’re more likely to hear grumbling about power bills than excitement about the future.

A quiet coalition of technologists, investors, and former internet builders is hoping to change all that.

Their ideas have been laid out in a limited edition hardcover book from American Transmission Leadership and Security, or ATLAS, a group that wants to rally thought leaders across the nation to rethink how America builds and regulates its power grid for the next century.

Copies were signed and handed out to a select group of tech movers and shakers at an after-hours private party during the Wyoming Blockchain Symposium.

Held at Jackson Hole’s Caldera House, the invitation-only gathering was a small affair with big ambitions, offering heavyweight ideas to heavy hitters invited to be part of the audience.

Cowboy State Daily was one of the only media outlets invited to attend the event, which included off-record presentations from HUT8Corp Founding Chairman and venture capitalist Bill Tai, Google Energy Market’s Kaitlin Savage, and Priority Power’s Kevin Young. Priority Power is a major energy solutions and transmission management provider in North America.

From Information To Knowledge

Tai is a heavy hitter in digital asset circles. He was a founding investor for several tech giants, including Zoom, Canva, Twitter (Tweetdeck), Wish.com and Coinbase.

More recently he’s backed several blockchain, AI, and deep-tech infrastructure projects.

Tai agreed to speak to Cowboy State Daily after the private party about what America’s energy grid needs in the next century to continue leading the world, as well as how a brave new digital asset world could benefit Wyoming.

“The American economy has gone through many transformational phases, dating back from an agricultural era and transforming to a mechanized Industrial Revolution to a second Industrial Revolution around information,” he said. “Now we are at the cusp of a new information economy, based on knowledge.”

This new knowledge-based economy is being layered on top of the information structure built into the Internet by companies such as Google, whose focus is easier access to information.

“With the advent of GPUs from NVIDIA or a handful of others, that information can be distilled into knowledge,” Tai said. “So you’re not just having to look at 50,000 articles and figure out what is most relevant to you. The machines basically sort things out and distill it into actions for you or things you can take actions on. The efficiency of that, I think, can unlock another layer of productivity that we haven’t seen before.”

The ‘Ma Bell’ Problem

The power needs for this next-era Information Age will be exponentially higher, Tai acknowledged, but he believes it doesn’t have to be done in a way that hurts the wallets of everyday citizens.

Behind the scenes, Tai and others talk about three big changes they believe are unavoidable if America is going to keep pace.

These are fixing interconnection bottlenecks, squeezing more power through lines we already have, and modernizing how we price and move electrons.

It’s basically the old “Ma Bell” problem, a reference to the 1990s breakup of Bell Telephone into multiple “Baby Bells” to more efficiently accommodate innovations in the telecommunications industry such as cell phones.

Right now, interconnection studies and transmission are still being controlled by incumbent monopolies, working under rules written for a much simpler grid.

That has developers waiting years and spending millions just to be told what it will cost them to connect — and those numbers can still change halfway through construction.

Tai and others want clearer, time-bound rules for grid studies, and more open-access-style markets that reward projects that actually relieve congestion and improve reliability, instead of just preserving old monopolies.

They’d also like to see the use of things like advanced conductors, which can make it possible for existing lines to safely carry more capacity than they do now.

Tech giants like Google are already quietly backing some of these “advanced” conductors companies.

Some in the Atlas circle also talk about treating electricity a little more like data.

That way, it could be broken into smaller “packets” that can be priced and steered in real time.

Blockchains, which are an indelible digital diary of transactions, could be used to track who used what and when, and reward people and communities that help balance the grid, instead of leaving all the decisions to complicated and time-consuming utility rate cases.

New Tools For Old Wires

The group also believes that cost efficiencies that kick in at larger sizes — so-called economy of scale — can be leveraged to keep costs lower for consumers.

That’s already worked in some communities to lower electric rates.

Indiana Michigan Power, for example, leveraged incoming data center revenue to offset infrastructure costs, executing a 3.6% rate reduction and saving average residential customers about $6 a month.

Georgia Power, after a multi-year rate freeze, has projected average residential savings of $102 annually in 2028, thanks to economies of scale from the buildout for massive industrial loads.

Pacific Gas & Electric in California has estimated system-wide rates are up to 11% lower than they would have been, thanks to fixed-grid maintenance costs being spread across more total megawatt hours sold.

“GPUs need electricity to run,” Tai said. “And while we can make all the GPUs you want, and we’re dominant in that industry, if you can’t plug them in, it doesn’t matter. America’s been in the lead in so many evolutions of this economy, and I’d like to see it stay that way. But, we’re at a point where we’re suffering from an inability to keep up with other countries in energy production.”

A New Kind Of Energy Export

In Wyoming, those kinds of arguments face a century or so of lived experience with coal, oil and gas.

People in the Cowboy State have some experience with what happens when far-off investors decide their energy is a commodity to be bought and sold.

As recent public meetings about data centers have shown, many are concerned that AI “gigafactories” and Bitcoin mines are just the next outsider bidding up a finite pool of energy molecules — and likely leaving locals holding the bag.

Tai doesn’t dismiss such worries. But he said he believes the risk of doing nothing is greater, and sees ways that Wyoming can leverage the influx to create new opportunities.

“More demand is better if it’s in concentrated chunks,” he explained. “Because you have to draw that capital investment. Because, if you have a little neighborhood that wants to increase energy by 10%, nobody cares, but if you have a big data center that wants to get set up and somebody can then draw the capital to fulfill that need, there will be excess energy.”

Such outsized demand will overcommit rather than undersize, Tai explained, leading to excess capacity.

That, in turn, helps boost the localized supply, helping to drive lower rates.

In his view, if Wyoming can attract large, long-term digital loads on the right terms — and pair them with smart grid upgrades — the state can both protect households and lock in a new export industry based on electrons for power, not just its raw commodities.

Wyoming’s Next Move

The ATLAS project, including the book it has recently produced, is intended to help start conversations with thought leaders in all industries about the changes this next-level information era is going to require.

“We need to make some fundamental changes to how we govern, how we regulate, and how we construct our next-generation (energy) production and grid,” Tai said.

For Wyoming, those conversations aren’t theoretical anymore.

Cheyenne already has roughly 15 data centers either operating or under construction, and dozens more inquiries that range from serious to tire-kickers.

Casper, Evanston, and other areas of the state, meanwhile, also have one or more data centers knocking at their doorsteps.

The state is already feeling the pressure that comes with digital-age industries that might want anywhere from 1GW to 10GW for a single facility.

Tai’s argument is that, with the right rules and upgrades, Wyoming can turn the pressure into an advantage — using large, long-term power contracts to justify new infrastructure that ultimately lowers costs for everyone else.

Skeptics might not be so sure — as recent fights showing up in public hearings and neighborhood meetings across the state show.

But the race to rebuild America’s grid is already, in some respects, off to the races to capture their slice of this emerging new economy.

What Wyoming ultimately decides to do about that will determine how big its own slice of the new information age becomes — and likely will shape its economic opportunities for generations.

Contact Renee Jean at renee@cowboystatedaily.com

description:

“Our administration is taking direct action and using every tool available by investing in Maryland-generated solar energy to lower costs and protect our environment,” said Gov.
Each year, the Maryland state government will buy 250,000 megawatt-hours of electricity from the project.
International precedents demonstrate how former mining lands can be repurposed into large-scale clean energy hubs.
Meanwhile, Germany’s Cottbus Ost Solar Park turns a former open-pit lignite mine into an artificial lake featuring a massive floating solar array.
text:
In Western Maryland, coal is giving way to clean sun.

In a major move for state finances and climate strategy, Governor Wes Moore announced a deal to power Maryland’s future by building on its industrial past. The state has locked in a 20-year Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with REV Renewables that turns a reclaimed coal mine in Garrett County into a massive solar hub.

It will help save money and slash emissions.

The Board of Public Works gave its green light to the historic contract, which will purchase clean energy directly from the upcoming 300-megawatt Jade Meadow III Solar Project. Department of General Services (DGS) officials project that the agreement will save taxpayers between $298 million and $515 million over two decades by hedging against volatile fossil fuel markets.

Site preparation and major construction are targeted to begin in 2026, leading toward commercial operation and grid delivery in 2028.

“Our administration is taking direct action and using every tool available by investing in Maryland-generated solar energy to lower costs and protect our environment,” said Gov. Moore.

“This agreement is a major win for Maryland, ensuring our state has access to reliable, clean sources of energy, progressing our clean energy goals, and advancing towards a more sustainable future.”

More from Energy

See All

Land re-use

This landmark agreement serves as a direct catalyst for Maryland’s mandate to achieve 100% clean electricity by 2035 and comply with its Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS).

Each year, the Maryland state government will buy 250,000 megawatt-hours of electricity from the project. It would be enough to power 20,000 homes. The deal instantly doubles the amount of green energy the state buys directly. It will cover nearly 15 percent of Maryland’s entire government portfolio.

Apart from the balance sheet, the location itself carries immense symbolic weight. Repurposing a reclaimed coal mine in Garrett County breathes new life into a former industrial brownfield site where redevelopment is highly difficult.

This sustainable and strategic placement avoids taking valuable agricultural farmland out of production, allowing Maryland to expand its clean energy footprint without sacrificing local farming assets.

Old coal mines and power plants already have grid interconnections, roads, and high-voltage power lines nearby, saving millions in transmission buildout costs.

Creating jobs for future

Department of General Services Secretary Atif Chaudhry framed the purchase as a model of smart stewardship while anchoring the state’s broader transition away from legacy fossil fuels.

“By locking in long-term renewable energy pricing for the next 20 years, we are not only protecting the State from future energy market volatility, but also securing approximately $300 million in savings for Maryland,” said Chaudhry.

The project builds on previous state initiatives like Mount St. Mary’s Solar and the Pinnacle wind farms.

During peak development, the project is expected to create more than 1,200 jobs across engineering, site management, trade labor, and technical design.

International precedents demonstrate how former mining lands can be repurposed into large-scale clean energy hubs. In China’s Ningxia region, the Ningdong Solar Park sits atop vast coal mining subsidence zones, tapping into thousands of megawatts of solar capacity directly over collapsed underground mines. Meanwhile, Germany’s Cottbus Ost Solar Park turns a former open-pit lignite mine into an artificial lake featuring a massive floating solar array.

Both projects showcase how legacy industrial sites can be re-engineered into multi-use renewable infrastructure without consuming valuable agricultural land.

text:
Despite this summer bringing hours of sunshine, many Britons have been unable to cash in on free electricity generated by the sun. Rooftop solar panels are usually out of the question if you live in a flat or rent your home, and the cost has made them prohibitive to many more households.

However, this could be about to change because next week the first wave of low-cost “plug-in” solar panels will go on sale in Great Britain.

Also known as “plug‑and‑play” or “balcony” solar, the clue to what makes them different is in the name: you can fix them to a balcony or garden wall, then plug them in like a toaster.

The mini solar systems are a familiar sight on balconies in Spain and in Germany, where they are known as a Balkonkraftwerk (balcony power plant), but until a recent change in the law, they were not permitted in Britain.

Matt Parry from the Renewable Energy Association, a trade body for renewable energy, says the kits are a gamechanger. “It democratises solar and gives everyone the chance to get it,” he says.

How the kits work

Unlike traditional rooftop solar panels, which require a professional to install, balcony solar kits – which commonly include one or two panels – can be plugged in to a three-prong wall socket.

You can fix them on a balcony railing, shed roof or garden wall – anywhere with good sun exposure and safe access.

When sunlight hits the solar panels, they generate a direct current. The microinverter then converts this to an alternating current, which flows into your home’s electrical system, reducing the amount you draw from the grid.

Previously, rules around the installation of solar were what was holding people back. But last year the government announced it would make it possible for plug-in solar to be used in this country.

To make this a reality, it has updated wiring regulations to allow households in Great Britain to connect plug-in solar panels capable of generating up to 800 watts of power into the mains without the need for an electrician. (The rules are different in Northern Ireland.)

Buying panels

Big names including B&Q, Currys, Lidl, Wickes and Amazon are lining up to sell plug-in solar.

Given the size (and weight) of these devices, it is expected that many will be bought online.

Although you may have already come across plug-in solar panels for sale, industry experts suggest waiting until the regulations take effect on 27 August before making a purchase.

Electrical Safety First, the consumer safety charity, is urging shoppers to stick to reputable high street retailers and their websites to ensure the device complies with the rules.

Luke Osborne, the charity’s technical director, advises people to “avoid buying these devices from third-party sellers on online marketplaces. These platforms are now not legally responsible for the safety of goods sold via their sites, exposing people to substandard versions that may put you and your home at risk.”

Andrew Moore, the founder of the British solar panel brand UKSOL, says: “We are working towards making the initial products available from 27 August.”

His company will initially sell 460W and 890W kits, starting at £599 and £999 respectively, and it plans to launch another four models in late September, with prices starting from £499.

Sizewise, plug-in solar setups are usually smaller than rooftop options, but sizes vary. The UKSOL 460W single panel kit measures 1,762mm x 1,134mm x 30mm and weighs 25.5kg. The 890W kit comprises two panels.

Setting up

The official guidance suggests that it will take about an hour to set up your system. It estimates 15-25% of people will need professional support mounting the panels, and about 15% will need minor electrical works. UKSOL suggests it takes two people to handle and position the panels, as each one weighs 25kg.

Osborne says plug-in solar systems should not be connected via extension leads, cable reels, multiway adaptors, travel adaptors or plug-in RCD adaptors. “These accessories can overheat, become overloaded and create additional safety risks,” he says.

There is also some other housekeeping. The owner has to tell their distribution network operator that they are using them (there should be a form in the box). You can find out who it is by inputting your postcode on the Energy Networks Association website. You will also be able to consult the ENA’s Connect Direct site for a list of approved devices, which is a good place to start before you buy.

Savings

Plug-in systems are about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar system, which means they will not provide enough energy to power a home on their own – but they could cut your bill.

One drawback is that you need to be home to use the power generated because without a battery it is not being stored for later, so flows back to the grid.

However, the adoption of balcony solar could, in time, pave the way for plug-in batteries in British homes, too. If paired with a plug-in solar system, households could store their own renewable electricity during the day and use it to run their appliances in the evenings. The government is reportedly considering plans to bulk-buy the devices and distribute them to low-income homes.

A basic plug-in solar system costs about £400. Parry says it will “give you back, at worst, £40 a year, and at the best about £110. If it’s the worst-case scenario, it’s going to pay for itself in 10 years, but at the best-case scenario, it’s four.

“If you’ve just got 800W, it’s only at its very peak that it will give you that.”

He adds: “The slight downside is that plug-in solar is hitting the markets as the summer’s coming to an end. It’s going to be more use in May next year.”

Moore says that the level of saving is affected by a number of things, including the system size, location, orientation and actually being home to use the power.

He expects the 460W system his company will be selling to save a typical household about £80-£120 a year, “while the 890W system could save more”.

He adds: “The greatest savings are achieved when households use appliances during daylight hours, as this increases the proportion of generated electricity used within the home.”

You can buy a more expensive 2,000W kit (the inverter will only allow 800W through) to maximise your power-generating capacity, but these are more expensive.

Staying safe

Although there is no obligation to do this, before buying a kit, some experts think you should get your home electrics checked by a professional. That is because this is the first time that British residential wiring circuits will take power in via a three-point socket rather than simply being used to distribute electricity.

Electrical Safety First is concerned about the impact on residual current devices, or RCDs, which sit in a household electricity box and cut off the power if someone drills through a wire or runs their lawnmower over a power cord. Electricians are concerned they may burn out when plug-in solar panels start adding electricity to the circuit.

A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson says: “Plug-in solar panels will be available to buy this summer, and stringent verification and registration checks are already in place. They are a transformative technology that can save people hundreds of pounds on their bills.”

Box] Renters

Plug-in solar should make it easier for tenants to take advantage of renewable energy, as any kit they buy can be moved from place to place.

But if you are renting, you should ask permission from your landlord before you invest in any panels.

The rules on what you can do with regard to fixing brackets to hold them, for example, may vary depending on what your tenancy agreement says.

There’s “no reason” why your landlord should be against the idea, Parry says. “He or she can look at the information and know it’s super, super safe.”

Meera Chindooroy, the deputy director of campaigns, public affairs and policy at the National Residential Landlords Association, says that while the organisation supports the “principle of tenants benefiting from plug-in solar panels … landlords would first need to be satisfied that the panels meet all required safety standards”.

text:
Duke Energy Progress is asking North Carolina regulators to raise electric rates on 1.6 million households in the eastern part of the state and the Asheville area. The utility scaled back its original ask after months of pushback, but some state officials say the compromise still costs customers too much.

Here are key takeaways:

Duke Energy Progress is now asking the North Carolina Utilities Commission to raise electric bills by 6.8% across all customer categories, or 9.3% for residential customers, over the next two years — down from an initial request of more than 15% across all categories, or 18% for residential customers.

The average household would see a $9.62 increase on monthly bills starting in January, followed by an additional $5.89 monthly increase beginning in January 2028.

The compromise requires Duke to refund customers $120 million from clean energy tax credits and put $10 million toward energy assistance funds for low-income customers.

Attorney General Jeff Jackson refused to sign onto the deal, saying in a statement that the rate increase is “still too high for families and still more than the company needs to cover its investments.”

Duke Energy Progress and its western counterpart, Duke Energy Carolinas, are set to merge into one combined utility by Jan. 1, making these the last rate cases the two negotiate separately.

Duke lowers rate ask after months of pushback

Duke Energy Progress agreed this month to a compromise with North Carolina’s Public Staff, the state’s utility watchdog group. In the new settlement, Duke will cut its proposed two-year rate increase from 18% to 9.3% for residential customers, and will lower its requested profit margin.

The settlement also blocks Duke from funding some administrative costs through the rate case, including portions of aviation, board and top-executive expenses, and requires it to set up a new fund for low-income customers.

The reduction follows intense criticism from customers and state leaders after Duke Energy reported $5 billion in profits in 2025 and its strongest second quarter ever.

FULL STORY: https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/article316831479.html

Duke and NC watchdog reach compromise, but critics push back

At a Utilities Commission hearing in Raleigh on Tuesday, Aug. 11, Duke executives defended the scaled-back rate hike request as a fair balance between reliability and affordability. State Rep. Maria Cervania, a Cary Democrat, warned that families are already stretched thin and face possible power disconnections.

Jackson credited the state’s Public Staff for pushing Duke to make concessions but said the deal still asks too much of customers.

text:
The U.S. government is aiming for a major solar breakthrough: utility-scale projects that can generate electricity for just 3 cents per kilowatt-hour by 2030 without relying on subsidies, according to PV magazine.

If that target is met, it would cut solar's cost in half from its 2017 benchmark and make it one of the cheapest sources of new power in the country.

Here's what to know

In 2017, unsubsidized utility-scale photovoltaic electricity cost about $0.06 per kilowatt-hour. The U.S. Department of Energy's Solar Energy Technologies Office wants to cut that figure to $0.03 by 2030, a price that would make solar cheaper than the operating costs of most fossil fuel generators and one of the lowest-cost options for expanding electricity supply.

The effort builds on the earlier SunShot Initiative, launched in 2011, when solar supplied less than 0.1% of the U.S. grid and total installed capacity was just 3 gigawatts. By 2017, cumulative installations had climbed past 47 gigawatts and were supplying more than 1% of national demand.

That first phase brought steep price declines. Utility-scale solar dropped from $0.28 per kilowatt-hour to $0.06, reaching the initial 2020 goal three years ahead of schedule. Residential solar went from $0.52 to $0.16 per kilowatt-hour, while commercial solar fell from $0.40 to $0.11.

Going solar is also one of the best ways for households to save money on home energy. Homeowners can explore EnergySage to get free solar installation estimates and compare quotes.

More background

Federal tax policy is shifting. With federal Investment Tax Credits and Production Tax Credits moving through phaseout and sunset schedules, the solar industry is under increasing pressure to reach cost parity without subsidies sooner than many analysts once expected.

The DOE is also looking beyond standard solar panels. For concentrating solar power, the agency is targeting $0.05 per kilowatt-hour for baseload systems with at least 12 hours of thermal storage and $0.10 per kilowatt-hour for peaking systems with fewer than six hours of storage.

Battery costs are another major part of the equation. Federal roadmaps aim for eight-hour battery storage systems to reach $100 per kilowatt-hour by 2040, and modeling suggests that pairing low-cost solar with storage at that price could allow solar-plus-battery systems to provide a dominant share of U.S. electricity by 2050.

What's being done?

To help reach those goals, federal agencies are funding advanced manufacturing and programs centered on thin-film tandem solar cells, cheaper silicon wafers, and modules that generate more electricity per panel. They are also supporting grid-forming inverters, power-flow modeling, dynamic controls, and interconnection tools so utilities can reliably handle larger amounts of solar and storage.

For homeowners considering rooftop panels, EnergySage's solar map shows the average cost of a home solar panel system on a state-by-state level, along with details on solar panel incentives in each state. Together, those resources can help readers get the best price for rooftop solar panels and access available incentives.

EnergySage's free services can also make the shopping process less overwhelming for people comparing installers and financing options. text:
The Environmental Protection Agency is once again changing America's gasoline rules in an effort to increase fuel supplies and bring down prices at the pump. This time, it means allowing more volatile gasoline to reach consumers earlier than it normally would.

Beginning September 1, the EPA will temporarily relax federal gasoline volatility requirements, effectively bringing winter-grade fuel into the market roughly two weeks before the summer control season normally ends on September 15. The agency says the move could add hundreds of thousands of barrels of gasoline per day to the available domestic supply.

The downside is that winter gasoline is more volatile, meaning it evaporates more readily. That characteristic helps engines operate in cold weather, but during hot conditions, additional fuel vapors can contribute to ground-level ozone and smog.

The EPA says it issued the emergency waiver after consulting with the Department of Energy and determining that unusual fuel-supply circumstances justified the move under the Clean Air Act. It's the latest in a series of fuel waivers the agency has used throughout 2026 as it tries to keep gasoline supplies up and prices down.

Why Summer And Winter Gas Are Different

Gasoline formulations change throughout the year largely because temperature affects how readily fuel evaporates. Volatility is commonly measured using Reid Vapor Pressure, or RVP, with higher numbers indicating gasoline that evaporates more easily.

Summer gasoline is formulated with a lower RVP because high temperatures already encourage evaporation. Reducing volatility helps limit emissions of volatile organic compounds, which can react with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form ground-level ozone.

Winter gasoline can have a higher RVP because colder temperatures make fuel less prone to evaporating. Allowing that higher-volatility gasoline onto the market early can increase supply flexibility, although doing so while temperatures remain high comes with an environmental tradeoff.

The EPA Says More Gasoline Should Mean Lower Prices

According to the EPA, its September waiver will allow E10 gasoline containing 10 percent ethanol to be sold at a higher RVP. The agency estimates that ending summer-blend requirements early will increase domestic gasoline availability by hundreds of thousands of barrels per day.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the move is intended to "increase supply and lower gas prices," while Energy Secretary Chris Wright similarly argued that expanding gasoline supply should provide relief for American families.

Exactly how much motorists will save isn't specified. Pump prices depend on numerous factors beyond fuel-blend requirements, including crude oil prices, refinery output, transportation costs, regional inventories, and taxes, so the waiver doesn't guarantee a particular reduction.

The Environmental Tradeoff

The reason these restrictions exist in the first place is air quality. Higher-volatility gasoline evaporates more readily in warm weather, potentially increasing the emissions that contribute to ozone formation.

September can still bring high temperatures across large parts of the country, particularly in southern and western states, which means pulling winter-grade gasoline forward could increase emissions compared with keeping the normal summer requirements in place.

EPA is also waiving state-level controls in Texas, Arizona, and California that ordinarily extend beyond September 15. Those exemptions can remain in effect for up to 20 days, with the agency saying it will continue monitoring fuel supplies and could issue additional waivers if necessary.

This Isn't The First Fuel Rule Change Of 2026

The September change follows several emergency measures already introduced this year. EPA says nationwide waivers have been in effect since May 1, with subsequent extensions changing ethanol-blending and gasoline-volatility restrictions.

Under its August 20 action, the agency also extended provisions allowing gasoline containing up to 15 percent ethanol and reinstated a one-psi RVP allowance for ethanol blends in states where it had previously been removed. Existing volatility waivers continue through August 31 before the wintertime limits are brought forward beginning September 1.

text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Nearly 200 activists in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement are criticizing President Donald Trump’s promotion of coal to fuel the rise of artificial intelligence data centers, according to a letter sent Friday.

The letter, signed by at least two former staffers from Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, marks the first major MAHA movement mobilization over fossil fuels and the latest in a series of rifts between the diverse group of activists and the Trump administration over environmental policy.

The letter to Trump, Kennedy and various other Cabinet officials, first obtained by The Associated Press, laments a 2025 executive order that aimed to boost coal to power data centers over pollution concerns and asks the administration to consider renewable options, including solar and geothermal energy.

“We understand the importance of American leadership in artificial intelligence, national security, innovation, and economic growth,” the letter reads. “But American AI leadership should not come at the cost of a more toxic burden for American children.”

In response, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers noted that greenhouse gas emissions dropped to a 30-year low during Trump’s first term and said Trump “was given a mandate to roll back the radical climate policies that are burning a hole through taxpayers’ wallets.”

The agencies receiving the letter didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Prominent MAHA figures behind the letter include Zen Honeycutt, a former Kennedy campaign staffer and founder of the advocacy group Moms Across America, and Charles Eisenstein, a former speechwriter on Kennedy’s campaign. Honeycutt said she asked the Kennedy-aligned political action committee MAHA Action to sign onto the letter but did not receive a reply.

Although it may not reflect the views of all MAHA activists, the new line of criticism against one of the administration’s signature policies less than three months before November’s midterm elections could present another challenge for Republicans as they seek to win over the voting bloc in key races.

As health secretary, Kennedy has carried out several policy changes that cater to the MAHA movement, including attempting to scale back childhood vaccine recommendations, a central priority for some activists. He also has sought to remove artificial dyes from food and encouraged Americans to have healthy diets free of ultraprocessed foods.

But many in the MAHA movement, which Trump credits with helping him win back the White House two years ago, say they have grown frustrated with the administration over its embrace of pesticides such as glyphosate and its deregulatory environmental agenda. Some have said they plan to vote on issues over party this fall, raising the political stakes of their increasingly public tensions with the Republican administration.

As president, Trump has enthusiastically embraced what he calls “big, beautiful coal” despite outcry from environmentalists about planet-warming greenhouse gases and toxic chemicals released by coal-fired power plants.

His administration has moved to reverse tighter Biden-era standards on greenhouse gas emissions, which, in addition to their climate impacts, can harm brain development in children and increase rates of heart attacks in adults.

He also has been a vocal advocate for data centers, which power artificial intelligence and cloud computing, framing them as a necessary component of winning the AI race against China.

“If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state, and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data center,” Trump said this week, “I would absolutely want it because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous.”

Data centers have become a political flashpoint in this year’s elections. Voters across the political spectrum have criticized them for jacking up electricity bills, draining water supplies, and creating unhealthy amounts of air and noise pollution.

Friday’s letter asks the administration to require transparent review of data center location and power sourcing decisions, and respect existing environmental review requirements in the permitting process.

Honeycutt said that after Trump’s executive order last year, she researched the impact of coal ash on communities and was disturbed by what she found. She said she was also concerned about other aspects of data centers, including their land use and their effects on the people living near them.

“The data center push has been an overwhelmingly negative impact on our communities, and there are many in the MAHA movement that are extremely disappointed about that,” she said. “We vote for those who put health and safety first.”

____

Associated Press writer Michael Phillis in Washington contributed to this report.

text:
LG Energy Solution says the unsolved problem in solid-state batteries is making large cells at scale, and expects the technology to reach smartphones roughly a decade before electric vehicles. Europe’s first solid-state gigafactory broke ground in France in February.

The company that has just opened America’s newest battery plant does not think solid-state cells are close for cars. “The problem with solid state is large-scale production,” said Robert Lee, North America president of LG Energy Solution, at a media roundtable at its new Lansing factory.

The difficulty scales with the cell. Small formats reach good energy density, Lee said, but “if you’re making very large form factors, most companies are struggling.”

His ordering of the market is the blunt part. Solid-state will appear in smartphones “probably a decade before you would see it in EVs,” with specialised applications arriving before either cars or grid storage.

Europe is building on the opposite assumption. ProLogium broke ground in February on a 12 GWh solid-state plant in Dunkirk, and a Dutch startup won public money to develop a factory of its own.

European carmakers are further along in testing than in production. Mercedes ran a prototype EQS almost 750 miles on cells from Factorial Energy, BMW has put a Solid Power pack in an i7, and Stellantis is testing a pack in a Dodge Charger Daytona.

Two of those three are semi-solid rather than fully solid. That distinction is precisely the gap Lee is describing, and it runs through most of the promised launch dates in this field.

China is moving faster on paper. BYD, CATL, Geely and others are targeting pilot production of solid-state cells in 2027, with wider deployment hoped for by the end of the decade.

LG’s answer is to improve what already works. It is developing lithium manganese rich cells with General Motors that use far less nickel and cobalt, promising more than 400 miles of range from 2028 at roughly the cost of cheaper lithium iron phosphate packs.

It is also hedging across chemistries. The company is preparing 46-series cylindrical cells at its Arizona plant and running a sodium-ion pilot for storage, in a market where CATL commercialised sodium first.

For Europe the timing question matters more than the technology. The continent lost its own champion when Northvolt collapsed, and the plants now being built here belong to Taiwanese, Korean and Chinese companies.

Which makes Lee’s caution worth reading twice. If large-format solid-state cells are a decade out, Europe’s route back into batteries runs through incremental lithium-ion improvements it does not currently manufacture at scale.

title: A Brand New EV At Used-Car Prices Makes The VW ID.4 A Bargain Right Now - CarBuzz
description:
The bone in question comes VW ID.
VW Is Putting Its Focus Towards More Successful Models The ID.
The ID.4 was the second model to feature the designation, behind the ID.3 compact hatchback that arrived in 2019.
Check out this 2025 ID.4 Pro S RWD, which has just over 16,000 miles on its odometer, and is currently offered at $48,279 by CarGurus.
The ID.4 Works As A Practical Family SUV If you're interested in an ID.4, it's likely you'll have a small family in tow.
text:
It has never been tougher for auto manufacturers to understand the right path to take when it comes to developing future models, primarily because there's so much financial uncertainty in the world. Electric vehicles were touted as the future of motoring, but the recent axing of government-sponsored incentives means that most are way too expensive for the average family to justify, leading to the recent explosion of hybrid and traditional ICE vehicles.

Still, those still interested in getting a slice of the EV life have been offered a bone by these recent events. The bone in question comes VW ID. 4-shaped.

VW Is Putting Its Focus Towards More Successful Models

The ID. family of models was VW's first push into the full EV market, a brave new world that would carry the automotive landscape into the next phase of its existence. The ID.4 was the second model to feature the designation, behind the ID.3 compact hatchback that arrived in 2019. The ID.4 compact crossover SUV was unleashed just a year later in 2020, and was expected to be one of VW's biggest sellers, given the strength of the crossover market.

Things looked to be going in the right direction initially, with sales in the US steadily increasing over its first few years on sale, with VW selling 37,789 specimens by 2023, an increase of over 84% when compared to the previous year. With EVs struggling to build in popularity though, this number slipped by 55% in 2024, before disaster struck towards the end of 2025. The Trump Administration announced that the useful EV federal tax credits, which knocked up to $7,500 off the price of new EVs, would be scrapped.

Suddenly, the US-built ID.4 was much more expensive. The rush to get one before the tax credits were axed in September 2025 saw ID.4 sales increase handily year-on-year, though the effects were made clear soon after. In Q4 2025, the first period following the departure of the tax credit, VW managed to sell just 248 cars. Extend that timeline to the first half of 2026, and ID.4 sales are down by a concerning 77.2%.

Seeing the writing on the wall early, VW ended production of the ID.4 in the US in April, the brand revealing that it had enough cars left over to stretch well into 2027 at the current demand.

VW took these measures to prioritize production of the 2027 Atlas SUV at its Chattanooga plant, an internal combustion-engined model that has brought the brand far more success and profit in recent times. The German giant is working on a new ID.4 for the future, but for now you'll have to make do with leftover 2025 and 2026 examples should you fancy one.

Some Very Tempting Savings Can Be Found

Like many other manufacturers that have been affected by the loss of the federal EV tax credits, VW is trying to get its EV supply chain moving by offering massive discounts on its models to try and make up for the loss of the incentives.

On average, new EVs cost around $7k more than equivalent ICEs, which makes them generally worse deals given that they tend to not only provide less range, but are also more of a hassle to keep charged due to the relative lack of charging stations around the US. For reference, while new ICEs cost around $48,000 on average, brand-new EVs will set you back $55k.

The thing is, that includes widespread incentives that manufacturers are offering right now, and without them, EV averages would swell to well above $60k.

Should an ID.4 catch your eye, VW's latest discounts covering the model should prove interesting. Given the number of cars still left in the brand's reserves, you can select either a 2025 or 2026 model year machine. If you opt for the latter, you'll be able to take advantage of a $6,000 discount, which, for reference, will knock the price of a base Pro RWD specimen down from $45,095 to $39,095. By going for a better-equipped Pro S AWD, you can hand over $48,095, rather than its original $54,095 MSRP.

Even greater savings can be had if you select a 2025 vehicle, with VW offering $7,500 discounts. The discounted prices look even more tempting when you bear in mind that used cars, with around 15,000 miles on the clock, are going for about the same price. Check out this 2025 ID.4 Pro S RWD, which has just over 16,000 miles on its odometer, and is currently offered at $48,279 by CarGurus. If you opted for a brand-new 2025 example of the same spec directly from VW, you'd be paying just $42,695.

Don't hang about though, as this current deal will come to a close on August 31. It covers both cash and leasing arrangements.

The ID.4 Works As A Practical Family SUV

If you're interested in an ID.4, it's likely you'll have a small family in tow. If so, you'll be pleased to learn that the ID.4 is one of the most practical crossovers in its class. We found that there was plenty of room in the front and rear, while its trunk afforded more space than either the Ford Mustang Mach-E or Hyundai Ioniq 5. Its cabin also scored well for quality, as VW did a good job including softer and more premium-feeling materials where it mattered, while small details such as the ID. Light system lifted the feeling of class once you climb inside.

The seats also scored well for comfort, and the car was perfectly easy to drive, making it ideal for a range of driving scenarios. When it comes to family cars, reinventing the wheel tends to be a wasted approach, as those who buy them generally just want a car that works as they expect, and will prove dependable. The ID.4 delivers in this regard, with no nasty surprises waiting for you.

VW's Electric Crossover Is Perfectly Nippy

​​​​​​​This sentiment extends to the wider driving experience that the ID.4 provides. Depending on whether you opt for the RWD or AWD versions, the ID.4 feels perfectly adequate from a performance standpoint. The dual-motor AWD variant is quicker, since its powertrain arrangement pumps out 335 horsepower, whereas the single-motor RWD version gets 282 hp. Aside from also providing extra traction with its all-wheel drive setup, the AWD ID.4 also brings plenty of extra torque to the table, with its 536 lb-ft figure playing the RWD's 402 lb-ft.

Be warned though, as the heavier and more powerful AWD variant won't be able to travel as far on a single charge. While it can manage around 263 miles on a full run, which admittedly isn't great when compared to rivals like the Ioniq 5, the lighter RWD car can hit 291 miles before it needs plugging in. As far as the handling goes, don't expect anything groundbreaking.

The ID.4 comes with a Sport mode, though all it does is quicken up the throttle response, stiffen up the steering, and up the aggression of the braking system a little more than standard. It's not set up to be a performance car, but rather to provide a comfortable and consistent ride along a variety of roads. It works well on the road as a family cruiser, but expect the driving experience to be like a typical SUV once you start shifting; safe, predictable, and just a bit bland all round.

Considering the target market for the car though, most will find this is a perfectly adequate compromise.

Other SUVs Are Being Offered With Considerable Discounts

Should the ID.4 not tickle your fancy, then several other EV manufacturers have carrots to dangle in front of you. Hyundai recently cut the MSRP of its Ioniq 5 N by a full $6,000 to help make it look more attractive following the end of the government tax credit scheme, while sister brand Kia is pushing its EV9 SUV with its own tempting deal. Not only is the Korean marque offering a 0% interest deal over 60 months on the vehicle, but this can be twinned with a handy $5,000 discount.

Speaking of SUV concessions, you can also save $2,000 thanks to an incentive provided by Cadillac for its Optiq model. Plenty of other deals pop up every now and again as well, with one of the most notable being one that Chevrolet cast out with its Equinox SUV in April 2026. As long as you owned a General Motors-built car constructed later than 2012, you could have up to $10k off the price of an Equinox, with the highest bracket being offered with the range-topping RS variant.

Until manufacturers find a way to organically lower the prices of their models, or sales increase considerably at their current prices, such deals will crop up pretty often. As a result, if you have your eye on an EV that currently doesn't have any form of deal attached right now, just wait a while... you may find your patience will be rewarded.

text:
Though it may feel like you missed the boat on a home battery purchase when tax credits expired, their value still holds. The tax credit was just an incentive.

Home batteries are having a moment in the United States, with installations reaching a record in the first quarter of 2026.

That momentum shows plenty of homeowners still consider battery backup worth the investment, whether the household cares most about lowering bills, outage readiness, or added peace of mind.

Here's what to know

One reason for the buying rush appears to be the expiration of the Inflation Reduction Act's 30% tax credit for residential clean energy improvements at the end of 2025.

CNET said that installations in the first quarter of 2026 were up 86% from the first quarter of 2025.

"Some of that demand kind of bled over into the beginning of 2026," Wood Mackenzie senior research analyst Max Issokson said.

He expects the market to ease without the credit but not to the same degree as with solar panels.

Owner sentiment points in the same direction. Habitelligence's Home Battery Adoption survey found that 91% of homeowners with batteries said they would make the purchase again, per CNET.

"The reasons are part financial and part personal," Habitelligence founder Mike Lock said, per the outlet.

More background

Home batteries hold electricity until it is needed, adding a major benefit to solar installations that are otherwise real-time production only.

Stored power can be crucial during an outage, and it can also help households avoid buying electricity when rates are high.

Battery storage can be a strong tool for protecting your home during outages, lowering energy costs, and moving closer to off-grid living. It can also keep important appliances running without the fuel, fumes, and maintenance associated with a generator.

If you're comparing options, it may be worth exploring EnergySage for information about home battery storage options, including competitive installation estimates. EnergySage has teamed up with the electrification brand Qmerit to guarantee you get the best price on home battery storage solutions.

Another company worth a look is Pila, which offers plug-and-play batteries priced at a fraction of what whole-home backup systems cost.

What can be done?

For many households, the decision to buy depends largely on local utility policies and the likelihood of losing power. Time of use plans, virtual power plant programs, and net metering policies play a big part in the financial decision.

Batteries can be more attractive if you already have solar but receive limited value for sending excess electricity back to the grid or if your utility uses time of use pricing that gets more expensive later in the day.

They can also be especially valuable in regions with frequent outages or in areas where utilities run VPP programs that pay customers to share stored energy.

In Massachusetts, the ConnectedSolutions program brings in $1,200 per year to the average homeowner.

However, batteries are not an obvious win for everyone. If you have strong net metering, seldom experience outages, or do not have access to a rebate or utility incentive, the payoff may be tough to justify.

"Storage still comes at a price premium," Issokson said.

text:
RALEIGH — The Triangle has seen a surge in e-bike use in recent years, with Raleigh’s dockless bikeshare program recording more than 5,500 e-bike trips in a single month.

Under North Carolina law, an electric-assisted bicycle has fully operable pedals, a motor of no more than 750 watts and a maximum motor-powered speed of 20 mph on a level surface.

The growth has prompted local governments to address where e-bikes and similar vehicles can be ridden. In January, Wake Forest updated its rules to prohibit motorized scooters, electric bicycles and electric-assisted bicycles on sidewalks while allowing them on town greenways, parks and multiuse paths with a 10-mph speed limit. Holly Springs allows qualifying e-bikes on sidewalks, greenways and multiuse paths.

Raleigh has also used financial incentives to encourage purchases. The city reopened its E-Bike Rebate Program in May, offering $500 standard vouchers and $1,500 income-qualified vouchers for households earning no more than 80% of the area median income.

Recipients could use the vouchers at participating Raleigh bike shops, including Conte’s Bike Shop locations at Brennan Station and Ridgewood.

Conte’s has three Triangle locations — two in Raleigh and one in Cary. Its Ridgewood location has shifted its focus primarily to e-bikes, reflecting growing demand for electric-assisted cycling.

North State Journal spoke with Conte’s general manager Michael Frazier about the company’s history, the rise of e-bikes and cycling’s appeal.

Q: What is the backstory of Conte’s Bike Shop?

A: Charles R. Conte Sr. opened the first Conte’s family-owned bicycle store in Newport News, Virginia, in 1957. Conte, the son of Italian immigrants, was a machinist at a nearby shipyard when he opened the small neighborhood bicycle and repair shop.

He ran the shop based on his love of bicycles and his vision of providing personal service and top-quality products he could personally guarantee. Conte’s became known for providing customers with a buying experience designed to turn first-time customers into customers for life.

Conte’s Bike Shop has also been selected 10 times for the National Bicycle Dealers Association’s Top 100 Best Bicycle Retailers designation.

Q: Why did Conte’s decide to shift the Ridgewood location primarily to e-bikes, and what does that say about demand in the Triangle?

A: The decision to convert our Ridgewood location into an e-bike-specific store was a rather easy one. At the beginning of 2025, that location was selling almost twice as many electric bikes as “acoustic” bikes, and that trend grew stronger as the year went on.

It became clear that the wants and needs of our community were shifting in a more e-bike-centric direction. Whether it’s recreational, just for fun or more utilitarian and transportation-focused, there are now viable e-bike options for pretty much any type of riding.

Whether it’s local college students at Meredith, NC State and William Peace, young families with little ones who aren’t quite ready to ride their own bikes yet or active retirees who enjoy the hills more when they’re flattened out a little, the e-bike universe has something for everyone.

With demand continuing to grow in 2026, we transitioned our Ridgewood store into primarily an e-bike store, along with children’s bikes and a full-service department for both acoustic and electric bikes.

Our Brennan Station and Cary locations continue to stock a healthy mix of e-bikes and acoustic bikes, including hybrids, gravel, road, mountain and children’s bicycles.

We also share inventory between locations. If you’re shopping at Ridgewood and your dream bike is only in stock at our Williamsburg, Virginia, store, we’ll get it for you.

Q: Why do you think cycling becomes so addictive for people?

A: Cycling is the most fun cardio that I know of. There’s the wind in your face and the ability to see more, go farther, go faster and burn calories. There are also a ton of mental health benefits. It’s a proven stress reducer and, in my experience, a form of active meditation.

I’ve lived in Raleigh for 26 years, and when I arrived, I was introduced to what was already a world-class greenway system. It’s only gotten better and longer since then.

With our current 117 miles of paved greenway, you can safely go almost anywhere around Raleigh — the N.C. Museum of Art, Umstead State Park, Shelley Lake, downtown, the Neuse River and even Clayton.

As far as our urban areas are concerned, there were few, if any, bike lanes back in 2001. I’m of the opinion that Raleigh has done an amazing job of changing that, with a large number of bike lanes now running through residential areas, around NC State and through downtown.

title: Target has more than 600 roof panels across 21 stores that look like solar and make exactly ...
description:
Putting solar on a supermarket roof is about as controversial as putting a cart corral in the parking lot.
Shawn Holzschuh, Target’s director of refrigeration, told a Food Marketing Institute conference that the CO2 store in Texas “did not go supercritical once” the previous summer.
Condenser capacity went up 35 percent and average discharge pressure fell 35 psi on a day that peaked at 102°F.
Precooling added 25 to 30 kilowatts of condenser capacity.
Norway went the opposite way, standing 6,400 solar panels bolt upright on an Arctic cold store because flat glass under snow generates nothing.
text:
Putting solar on a supermarket roof is about as controversial as putting a cart corral in the parking lot. Big flat roof, big power bill, bolt the glass down, take the credit. Retailers have run that play for fifteen years and nobody blinks at it any more.

Target has been doing something stranger on 21 of its roofs. The hardware looks close enough to solar that you would walk straight past it, and it produces exactly zero watts.

The panels are mirrors. Water and glycol run through them in a sealed loop, and what comes back is colder than the air outside, in the middle of the afternoon, in Texas. The heat never reaches the parking lot. It leaves the atmosphere.

Target started testing them in 2021 and now has more than 600 installed across six states, with 16 more sites planned for 2026. Washington spent this summer making that a much less obvious decision than it looked a year ago.

The trick is a gap in the atmosphere about five microns wide

Everything on Earth radiates infrared, and most of it never gets anywhere, because water vapor and CO2 absorb it and hand it straight back. That is the greenhouse effect doing its job.

But the atmosphere has a blind spot. Between roughly 8 and 13 microns it is close to transparent, so anything radiating in that band is firing into deep space, which sits at about 3 kelvin and has never once sent anything back.

That is why frost forms on your windshield on nights the thermometer never hit freezing. The catch has always been daylight, when sunshine dumps roughly a kilowatt per square meter onto the same surface and swamps the effect.

A Stanford group cracked it in 2014. Aaswath Raman, Shanhui Fan and three colleagues stacked seven alternating layers of hafnium oxide and silicon dioxide into a film that reflects 97 percent of incoming sunlight while emitting hard through the 8-to-13 micron window.

Under direct sun above 850 watts per square meter, it settled 4.9 degrees Celsius below ambient and pulled 40.1 watts of heat per square meter. ARPA-E paid for the work, and it has been cited more than 3,300 times since.

Two of the authors, plus engineer Eli Goldstein, spun it out as SkyCool Systems in 2016, half an hour up the road in Mountain View.

The commercial version is not a photonic crystal grown in a nanofab. It is laminated plastic, US-made and PFAS-free, wrapped around a panel that behaves like a solar collector run backwards. The only electricity in the loop is a circulation pump.

Picking one narrow slice of the spectrum and ignoring the rest is the same logic behind those Swiss greenhouse modules that harvest only the infrared the tomatoes never use, aimed the other way.

Target has 600 of these and wants the condenser gone

A supermarket refrigeration rack spends its life fighting one number: how easily it can dump compressor heat outside. On a 100-degree afternoon the condenser fans are shoving hot air into hotter air, and the compressors work harder for less cooling.

SkyCool’s panels tie into that loop through a heat exchanger and do two jobs depending on the weather. Between about 60 and 85°F they subcool the liquid refrigerant, cutting flash gas and lifting capacity. Above 85°F they switch to precooling the condenser, dropping discharge temperature and taking load off the compressors.

The 21 stores are in California, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Nevada and Texas. Shawn Holzschuh, Target’s director of refrigeration, told a Food Marketing Institute conference that the CO2 store in Texas “did not go supercritical once” the previous summer.

That is a bigger deal than it sounds. Transcritical CO2 racks lose efficiency badly once ambient climbs past the critical point, which is the whole reason American grocers spent years calling CO2 a northern-climate refrigerant.

The hard numbers from a store in Roseville, California are more useful than the anecdote. That site runs R404a, and the array added 40 kilowatts of heat rejection into the condenser circuit. Condenser capacity went up 35 percent and average discharge pressure fell 35 psi on a day that peaked at 102°F.

The panels lie flat, which matters on a crowded roof for the same reasons it did with that flat-mounted solar array at a Fresno water plant. Tilt buys sun angle and costs steel, wind loading and square footage.

Holzschuh has said the panel system currently costs 10 to 20 percent more than simply replacing an air-cooled condenser, and that he expects the gap to close as manufacturing scales. The stated goal for 2026 is to put enough panels on one roof to delete the air-cooled condenser entirely.

California paid for the boring version, and the numbers held

Before Target, the California Energy Commission funded two supermarket installs and published the results. It is the least glamorous document in this story and easily the most useful, because a state agency has no reason to flatter anybody.

At a store in Red Bluff, an 80-panel array added 30 to 45 kilowatts of heat rejection, dropped compressor discharge pressure by 50 psi and cut refrigeration energy use by up to 15 percent. Peak demand came down 5 to 7 kilowatts.

The water number gets overlooked. That roof had a sprinkler soaking the condenser coils every summer to hold capacity up. With the panels in, the sprinkler came off and the site stopped spraying tens of thousands of gallons a year onto its own equipment.

At the second site, in Milpitas, a 60-panel array subcooled below 75°F and precooled the rest of the year. Subcooling added 10 to 25°F and cut energy use 15 to 20 percent. Precooling added 25 to 30 kilowatts of condenser capacity. Total saved: just under 20,000 kilowatt-hours.

Twenty thousand kilowatt-hours is not going to reorganize the grid. It is one grocery store. It is also a measured number in a government report rather than a projection in a pitch deck.

Washington just made the easy option easier

Here is where the story turned this summer. On July 27, a rewritten EPA rule took effect that pushes back nearly every deadline pressuring American grocers to abandon high-warming refrigerants.

Under the reconsidered Technology Transitions rule, supermarket systems now have until January 1, 2032 to hit the 150 or 300 GWP limits, five years later than the original schedule, with an interim ceiling of 1,400.

Cold storage warehouses got six years and an interim limit of 700. Remote condensing units got six years as well.

The rule also lets a supermarket raise cooling capacity by up to 15 percent without that counting as installing a new system, and EPA projects the revisions will save regulated industry more than $900 million against the 2023 version.

So the clock that was supposed to push American grocery chains onto CO2 and ammonia by 2027 has slipped to 2032. If you run a chain and wanted a reason to leave the old rack alone, there is now one in the Federal Register.

What did not change is the third pillar of the AIM Act, which caps how much HFC refrigerant can be produced or imported in the first place. That schedule still calls for a 40 percent cut through 2028, then 70 percent in 2029 and 85 percent in 2036.

Which is the actual argument for a mirror. The panels sit in a closed water-glycol loop and do not care what is in the pipe next to them, so the same array works on an aging R404a rack today and on a transcritical CO2 rack after the remodel.

Target’s engineers have made that reuse case publicly. The panels survive the refrigerant change. The condenser does not.

Cold storage is the bigger prize, and it is having a rough year

Supermarkets are the shop window. The roofs that would move the needle belong to refrigerated warehouses, which are enormous, flat, and already carrying industrial ammonia plants underneath.

Lineage is the largest operator on Earth and reported second-quarter results on August 5. As of June 30 it ran 498 facilities, about 87 million square feet and roughly 3.1 billion cubic feet of temperature-controlled space.

It also posted its first year-over-year rise in same-warehouse physical occupancy since going public, up 90 basis points to 75.8 percent, after the industry built far more capacity than demand between 2021 and 2025.

Lineage has idled 15 sites, ten last year and five this year, and plans to sell around $1 billion in assets to pay down debt.

That is exactly the balance sheet that makes a passive, no-fan retrofit interesting. When a quarter of your racking sits empty, energy cost per occupied pallet is the number that hurts. SkyCool says Lineage moves from pilot to enterprise-scale proof in the second half of 2026, which is now.

Cold-store roofs have turned experimental generally. Norway went the opposite way, standing 6,400 solar panels bolt upright on an Arctic cold store because flat glass under snow generates nothing.

Where the mirrors run out of road

Radiative cooling needs a dry sky. Water vapor absorbs inside the 8-to-13 micron window, so a panel in Houston in August performs nothing like a panel in Red Bluff, and cloud cover does the same thing. Nobody is putting these on a Seattle roof and calling it a chiller replacement.

Roof area is the other hard ceiling. A store can only reject as much heat as its square footage allows, and a 20 percent premium over a conventional condenser swap is real money across a national rollout.

SkyCool is also small. It says it closed 2025 at $3.33 million in revenue with $4.2 million of contracted backlog for 2026, across 30-plus installations. Those are company figures published in May through the investment platform Propel(x), not audited results, and they describe a business about the size of a regional HVAC contractor.

Worth being precise about the trophies, too. SkyCool was named one of 29 BNEF Pioneers finalists in February, out of more than 600 applications. It did not win. When BloombergNEF named the winners on April 20, the three data center slots went to Emerald AI, HT Materials Science and Point2 Technology.

The data center pitch carries the biggest number attached to any of this. BNEF expects data centers to draw 1,600 terawatt-hours a year by 2035, around 4.4 percent of global electricity, and every campus has to put its waste heat somewhere.

Rejecting it to space rather than into the air above the neighbors is at least a different answer. It is also a long way from a grocery loop, and pretending those are the same engineering problem would be generous.

The technology has one honest job right now, and it is not replacing air conditioning. It is making the condenser next to it smaller, or on a good roof in a dry climate, unnecessary.

Target says it intends to find out which of those it gets this year. That answer turns up on an electric bill in Texas around October, and it will be the least dramatic 15 percent anybody ever measured.

Pushback against the state’s largest-ever transmission lines is growing, with a group of Texas House members calling for utility regulators to pause the project until reforms can be made in the next legislative session.

The lawmakers filed the request for a delay less than an hour before the Public Utility Commission met Friday to discuss applications for projects under the $33 billion plan.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Known as the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, the initiative calls for construction of three new 765-kilovolt east-west transmission lines to help ensure there’s enough power to meet demand in the energy-rich region of West Texas.

But the way it has been carried out has sparked growing outrage from Texans concerned with a lack of transparency they say has left them with little recourse against projects that could destroy their land and livelihoods. That pushback now has the same lawmakers who in 2023 passed a measure calling for the reliability plan questioning the project.

“We agree that Texas’ growth and continued prosperity require a reliable electric grid, and that a reliable grid depends on both increased generation and transmission,” the lawmakers said in their letter. “We are prepared to work toward solutions that yield both in the 90th Legislative session.”

The letter, which was signed by 31 Texas House members, was filed with the PUC two days after a House committee meeting on the transmission line project drew Texans to rally against it. More people signed up to speak during public comment than could be heard in the allotted time.

PUC delays action on transmission line

On Friday, the PUC put off taking any action on the applications for the 765-kilovolt transmission line being built by Oncor in North Texas. Instead, the state regulatory agency said it will take time to deliberate the line, which is known as Dinosaur to Longshore, before bringing it up for discussion at a later meeting.

The PUC is scheduled to discuss the two other planned line projects, including the Howard-Solstice Line that would stretch from San Antonio through the Hill Country to Fort Stockton, next Friday. The high-voltage lines are all part of the reliability plan that was a result of House Bill 5066.

Article continues below this ad

That legislation was an effort to get ahead of a surge in energy demand that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas forecast could quadruple by 2032. The effort included shortening the deadline for the PUC to approve or deny applications for new transmission projects from one year to 180 days to help meet the rapidly growing energy demand.

But House members argued in the letter that “the bill did not contemplate 765-kilovolt lines and the 180-day timeline in the bill was never intended for projects running transmission lines all across the state.”

RELATED:Texas lawmakers turn against massive power lines they ordered after outcry

Now, the representatives are saying that there were “multiple failures of due process” that threaten landowners’ property rights and are asking the PUC to deny all Certificate of Convenience and Necessity applications, which utilities must file to build a new line, related to the proposed 765-kilovolt projects.

Article continues below this ad

Lawmakers seek changes to approval process

The call to pause the project echoes a stance that Sen. Charles Schwertner took last month after a 15-hour Senate Committee on Business and Commerce hearing that also drew a flood of negative comment.

Schwertner, who chairs the committee, said the process, lack of proper notice from utilities and shortened timelines for PUC proceedings and due process at the State Office of Administrative Hearings all raised “significant concerns.”

In a social media post after the hearing, he called on the state utility regulatory agency to deny existing applications to allow for the process to be reformed in the next legislative session “to ensure future projects are fair and transparent.”

PUC officials, representatives of manufacturers and energy industry leaders warned at Wednesday's hearing by the House Committee on State Affairs that delaying the project could be “catastrophic” for the Permian Basin, which, despite being an energy-rich area, is threatened by inadequate power supply.

“Every day we don’t make a decision on building transmission just exacerbates that issue,” PUC Chair Thomas Gleeson told the House committee.

West Texas energy operations already have faced challenges, said Todd Staples, president of the Texas Oil & Gas Association. He reminded lawmakers that operations in the Permian Basin shut down when they lost power during the winter storm of 2021 because they were not classified as critical infrastructure.

“The consequences of not getting this right are catastrophic,” he said.

But thousands of affected landowners have pushed back, with many saying the 180-day timeline from an initial utility filing to approval of a project didn’t allow time for them to understand, evaluate and effectively participate in the process.

A representative from the Office of Public Utility Counsel said Friday that the “largest obstacle” for the residential customers and small businesses that it represents was the “compressed timeline.”

text:
Though it may feel like you missed the boat on a home battery purchase when tax credits expired, their value still holds. The tax credit was just an incentive.

Home batteries are having a moment in the United States, with installations reaching a record in the first quarter of 2026.

That momentum shows plenty of homeowners still consider battery backup worth the investment, whether the household cares most about lowering bills, outage readiness, or added peace of mind.

Here's what to know

One reason for the buying rush appears to be the expiration of the Inflation Reduction Act's 30% tax credit for residential clean energy improvements at the end of 2025.

CNET said that installations in the first quarter of 2026 were up 86% from the first quarter of 2025.

"Some of that demand kind of bled over into the beginning of 2026," Wood Mackenzie senior research analyst Max Issokson said.

He expects the market to ease without the credit but not to the same degree as with solar panels.

Owner sentiment points in the same direction. Habitelligence's Home Battery Adoption survey found that 91% of homeowners with batteries said they would make the purchase again, per CNET.

"The reasons are part financial and part personal," Habitelligence founder Mike Lock said, per the outlet.

More background

Home batteries hold electricity until it is needed, adding a major benefit to solar installations that are otherwise real-time production only.

Stored power can be crucial during an outage, and it can also help households avoid buying electricity when rates are high.

Battery storage can be a strong tool for protecting your home during outages, lowering energy costs, and moving closer to off-grid living. It can also keep important appliances running without the fuel, fumes, and maintenance associated with a generator.

If you're comparing options, it may be worth exploring EnergySage for information about home battery storage options, including competitive installation estimates. EnergySage has teamed up with the electrification brand Qmerit to guarantee you get the best price on home battery storage solutions.

Another company worth a look is Pila, which offers plug-and-play batteries priced at a fraction of what whole-home backup systems cost.

What can be done?

For many households, the decision to buy depends largely on local utility policies and the likelihood of losing power. Time of use plans, virtual power plant programs, and net metering policies play a big part in the financial decision.

Batteries can be more attractive if you already have solar but receive limited value for sending excess electricity back to the grid or if your utility uses time of use pricing that gets more expensive later in the day.

They can also be especially valuable in regions with frequent outages or in areas where utilities run VPP programs that pay customers to share stored energy.

In Massachusetts, the ConnectedSolutions program brings in $1,200 per year to the average homeowner.

However, batteries are not an obvious win for everyone. If you have strong net metering, seldom experience outages, or do not have access to a rebate or utility incentive, the payoff may be tough to justify.

"Storage still comes at a price premium," Issokson said.
